q: Under which arrangement does the investment banker guarantee the issuer the full proceeds and absorb the loss on any shares it cannot sell?
o: Firm commitment underwriting
Best efforts underwriting
Private placement
Green shoe option
e: In a firm commitment the underwriter buys the entire issue at a set price and resells it, so any shares left unsold are its loss. Under best efforts the banker only tries to sell as much as possible and the company bears the shortfall.

q: Which of these fictional clients qualifies as an accredited investor under Rule 501 of Regulation D?
o: Ivan, net worth of $1.5 million, of which $700,000 is equity in his primary residence
Rosa and Tom, joint income of $320,000 in each of the last two years, expecting the same this year
Leah, single, income of $185,000 in each of the last two years and expecting a raise
A local charity whose total assets are $4 million
e: Natural persons qualify with joint income above $300,000 (or above $200,000 alone) in each of the two most recent years plus a reasonable expectation of the same (2026 edition figure), or net worth above $1 million excluding the primary residence. Charities need assets above $5 million.

q: A dealer quotes Harbor Corp. at $18.40 bid and $18.55 ask. A client sells 200 shares to the dealer. Which statement is correct?
o: The client receives $18.55 a share, since a dealer buys at its ask
The dealer is acting as the client's agent and earns a commission
The client receives $18.40 a share, since a dealer buys at its bid
The dealer is called a specialist because the trade is over the counter
e: A dealer is a principal who quotes a two-sided market: it buys at the bid and sells at the higher ask. On an exchange the dealer is a specialist; in the OTC market it is a market maker. A broker, by contrast, is an agent paid a commission.

q:
Which statements about venture capital are correct?
I. It typically finances privately held companies, often through convertible preferred stock.
II. It tends to have a low correlation with equities.
III. VC firms usually stay passive and avoid advising company management.
IV. Bridge financing is capital provided ahead of an expected IPO.
o: I and III only
II and IV only
I, II, III, and IV
I, II, and IV
e: Venture capital funds private companies (often with convertible preferred), is high risk/high return, illiquid, and has low correlation with equities. VC firms usually advise management and aim to exit in roughly 5–10 years, ideally by IPO. Bridge financing supports an expected IPO.

q: Marcus, 58, has moderate risk tolerance, wants diversification and professional management, and may need his money within a few years. A friend pitches an oil-and-gas limited partnership. What is the best advice?
o: Buy the LP, since limited partners decide when distributions are paid
Buy the LP, since partnership income is passed through to him tax-free
Favor a mutual fund or ETF; the LP is likely illiquid and its resale may be restricted
Join as the general partner, which limits his personal liability
e: LP interests are generally riskier than bonds or listed stocks, usually illiquid, give limited partners no management role, and may be hard to sell. Mutual funds or ETFs offer diversification and professional management with less marketability and liquidity risk, so LPs are generally unsuitable for the average investor.

q: Northgate Robotics sells new shares in its IPO at $20 each, paying underwriting costs of $1.40 a share. A week later, Kai buys 1,000 Northgate shares on the exchange at $26. How much of Kai's money goes to Northgate?
e: Only primary-market sales send money (less underwriting costs) to the issuer. Kai's purchase is a secondary-market trade between investors, so Northgate receives nothing: 1,000 × $26 = $26,000 goes to the selling investor.

q: Bianca sells short 300 shares of Lumen Co. at $60 with a 50% initial margin. Lumen pays a $0.80 per-share dividend before she covers, and she buys the shares back at $52. What is her percentage return?
e: Deposit = 300 × $60 × 0.50 = $9,000. Proceeds $18,000 − cost to cover $15,600 = $2,400 gain. Less dividend paid 300 × $0.80 = $240 → net profit $2,160. Return = $2,160 ÷ $9,000 = 24.00%.

q: Elena buys 500 shares at $48 in her margin account with a 50% initial margin. Her broker's maintenance margin is 30%. At about what share price will she receive a margin call?
e: Margin-call price = [purchase price × (1 − initial margin)] ÷ (1 − maintenance margin) = ($48 × 0.50) ÷ (1 − 0.30) = $24 ÷ 0.70 = $34.29.

q: Elena bought 500 shares at $48 on 50% initial margin, so she owes the broker $24 a share. The stock drops to $30 and the maintenance margin is 30%. How much cash must she deposit to restore the required equity?
e: Required equity = $30 × 0.30 = $9.00 a share. Actual equity = $30 − $24 loan = $6.00. Shortfall = $3.00 × 500 shares = $1,500.

q: Arjun buys 200 shares at $50 using 50% margin at 7% annual interest. During the year the stock pays a $1 per-share dividend, and he sells all shares at $58 at year-end. What is his holding period return?
e: Ending $11,600 − beginning $10,000 + dividends $200 − interest (7% × $5,000 loan) $350 = $1,450. His investment = 50% × $10,000 = $5,000. HPR = $1,450 ÷ $5,000 = 29%.

q: Noor owns 800 shares trading at $70. She wants out if the stock falls to $62, but will not accept any sale below $62, even if that means she may not get out. Which order fits?
o: Sell stop at $62
Sell stop-limit at $62
Buy stop at $62
Sell limit at $62
e: A stop-limit triggers at the stop price and then becomes a limit order, so it never fills below the limit. The trade-off: if the stock gaps through $62 and keeps falling, it may never execute. A plain stop becomes a market order and guarantees execution, not price.

q: Theo sold short 500 shares at $35 and wants to cap his loss if the stock rallies. Which order should he enter?
o: Sell stop at $30
Buy limit at $30
Buy stop at $40
Sell stop at $40
e: A short seller loses when the price rises, so protection is a buy stop placed above the current price. If the stock trades at or through $40, the order becomes a market order to buy and cover the 500 shares.

q: A brokerage firm holding a client's securities in street name goes bankrupt. Which statement about SIPC is correct?
o: It covers up to $250,000 per customer, all of which may be securities
It covers up to $500,000 per customer, including up to $250,000 of cash
It covers market losses incurred while waiting for securities to be returned
It covers only certificates held by the client, not street-name holdings
e: SIPC oversees the liquidation of failed brokerage firms and covers each customer up to $500,000, of which no more than $250,000 may be cash (2026 edition figure). It does not protect against market losses.

q: Celia asks which of her holdings can be cashed in quickly at a known value but has no market where she could sell it to another investor. Which holding fits?
o: Her 26-week Treasury bill
Her negotiable CD
Her bank money market deposit account
Shares of a privately held company
e: Liquidity means converting to cash quickly at a known price without significant loss of principal; marketability means being able to sell in an identifiable market. An MMDA is liquid but can only be redeemed with the bank, so it is not marketable.

q: Owen buys a 26-week Treasury bill with a $10,000 face value for $9,880 and holds it to maturity. What is his holding period return, and how is the $120 taxed?
o: 1.20%; ordinary income for federal tax only
1.21%; ordinary income for federal and state tax
1.21%; long-term capital gain for federal tax
1.21%; ordinary income for federal tax only
e: Income = $10,000 − $9,880 = $120. HPR = $120 ÷ $9,880 = 1.21%. The discount is interest: ordinary income for federal purposes, taxed at maturity, and exempt from state and local income tax.

q: Gwen is in a 24% federal and 6% state bracket (ignore any interaction between the two). She earns $500 of discount income on a T-bill and $500 of interest on a bank CD. How much more total income tax does the CD interest cost her than the T-bill income?
e: T-bill: federal only = $500 × 24% = $120. CD: federal and state = $500 × (24% + 6%) = $150. Difference = $150 − $120 = $30, the state tax the T-bill avoids.

q: A government securities dealer sells Treasuries to a money market fund for $4,990,000 and agrees to buy them back in 7 days for $5,000,000. What does the fund earn?
o: Nothing; the fund is the borrower and pays the dealer $10,000
A $10,000 capital gain, because the deal is legally a sale
$10,000 of interest, about 0.20% for the 7 days
$10,000 of interest, about 0.20% per year
e: A repo is essentially a collateralized loan from the buyer to the dealer. Interest = $5,000,000 − $4,990,000 = $10,000. Repo rate = $10,000 ÷ $4,990,000 ≈ 0.20% for the 7-day term.

q: Hal lives in a high-tax state and wants a money market fund whose income escapes both federal and his state's income tax. Which choice fits best?
o: A single-state tax-exempt fund for his state, noting AMT may apply to private activity bonds
A national tax-exempt fund, since all of its income is free of his state's tax
A Treasury-only taxable money market fund, since its income is free of federal tax
A bank money market deposit account, since FDIC-insured interest is tax-exempt
e: Single-state tax-exempt money market funds hold that state's municipal securities, so residents generally avoid both federal and state income tax. Income from any private activity bonds in the fund may be subject to the alternative minimum tax.

q: Why does commercial paper usually yield slightly more than a Treasury bill of similar maturity?
o: Its interest is exempt from state income tax
Its maturities commonly run up to two years
It is secured by the issuer's receivables and inventory
It is slightly less liquid and carries more default risk
e: Commercial paper is an unsecured, negotiable note from a large corporation, maturing in 270 days or less and often backed by bank credit lines. Versus T-bills it is a bit less liquid and riskier, so it pays a modestly higher yield.

q: A small U.S. importer can't get credit from its overseas supplier and is too small to issue commercial paper. Which money market instrument is built for this need?
o: Eurodollar CD
Banker's acceptance
Repurchase agreement
Negotiable CD
e: With a banker's acceptance, the importer's bank pays the foreign supplier and the importer repays the bank, typically within three to six months. The bank may sell the draft at a discount. Firms too small for commercial paper often use them.

q: Priya bought 200 shares of Delta Grid for $11,000. This year she sells all 200 for $8,200, and 18 days later she buys 200 Delta Grid shares for $8,600. What is her basis in the new shares?
e: Loss = $11,000 − $8,200 = $2,800. Buying back within 30 days (2026 edition figure) makes it a wash sale, so the loss is not recognized now. New basis = $8,600 cost + $2,800 disallowed loss = $11,400 ($57 a share).

q: Rina bought 100 more shares of a stock on March 1. On March 21 she sells 100 older shares of the same stock at a $1,500 loss. What is the tax result?
o: A $1,500 loss is allowed because the purchase came before the sale
No loss now, and the $1,500 is permanently lost
No loss now; the $1,500 reduces the basis of the March 1 shares
No loss now; the $1,500 is added to the basis of the March 1 shares
e: A wash sale occurs when similar securities are acquired within 30 days before or after a loss sale (2026 edition figure). The March 1 purchase is 20 days before the sale, so the $1,500 loss is deferred and added to the basis of those shares.

q: Leon has a $9,000 long-term gain, a $4,000 long-term loss, a $2,500 short-term gain and an $11,500 short-term loss this year. What is the result?
o: Deduct the full $4,000 net loss this year
Deduct $3,000 this year and forfeit the other $1,000
Deduct $3,000 this year and carry $1,000 forward
Deduct a $9,000 short-term loss and pay LT rates on $5,000
e: LT: $9,000 − $4,000 = $5,000 gain. ST: $2,500 − $11,500 = $9,000 loss. Cross-net: $5,000 − $9,000 = $4,000 net loss. Deduct $3,000 (2026 edition figure); carry the remaining $1,000 forward indefinitely.

q: Dmitri, a single filer, has MAGI of $230,000, including $45,000 of net investment income. Using the textbook's $200,000 threshold for single filers, what is his net investment income tax?
e: NIIT = 3.8% (2026 edition figure) × lesser of NII ($45,000) or MAGI over threshold ($230,000 − $200,000 = $30,000). Tax = 3.8% × $30,000 = $1,140.

q: Which cash dividend is most likely to qualify for the preferential 0%/15%/20% rates?
o: From a REIT whose shares the client has held for three years
From a C corporation stock held from 45 days before to 45 days after the ex-dividend date
From an S corporation in which the client owns shares
From a C corporation stock bought 10 days before and sold 20 days after the ex-dividend date
e: Qualified dividends come from C corporations (income taxed at the corporate level first) and require holding the stock more than 60 days during the 121-day period that starts 60 days before the ex-dividend date (2026 edition figure). Qualified dividends are taxed at 0%, 15% or 20%.

q: Pia sells shares of a gold ETF she held for three years at a gain. What is the maximum federal rate on that long-term gain?
e: Gold and silver ETFs are generally treated as collectibles, and long-term gains on collectibles (art, metals, gems, coins, stamps, antiques) face a maximum 28% rate (2026 edition figure), not the 0/15/20% rates.

q: Jae owns 100 shares with a $30 per-share basis and receives a $2 per-share distribution identified as a return of capital. What is the tax effect?
o: No current tax; his total basis falls to $2,800
$200 taxed as a qualified dividend; basis stays $3,000
$200 taxed as ordinary income; basis falls to $2,800
No current tax; his total basis rises to $3,200
e: A return-of-capital dividend is untaxed because it returns the investor's own money; instead it reduces basis. New basis = ($30 − $2) × 100 = $2,800.

q:
For a client who lives in State X, which statements are correct?
I. Interest on a U.S. Treasury note is federally taxable but exempt from state income tax.
II. Interest on a State X municipal bond is generally exempt from federal and State X income tax.
III. Interest on a State Y municipal bond is exempt from State X income tax.
IV. Interest on a corporate bond is taxable at both the federal and state level.
o: I and III only
II and III only
I, II, III, and IV
I, II, and IV
e: Treasury interest: federal yes, state no. Corporate interest: taxable at both levels. Municipal interest: generally federal-exempt, and state-exempt only for bonds issued in the investor's home state, which can make in-state munis double tax-exempt.

q: A bond's yield to maturity climbs from 4.10% to 5.35%. How large was the move in basis points?
o: 12.5 basis points
125 basis points
1.25 basis points
1,250 basis points
e: A basis point is 1/100 of 1%. Change = 5.35% − 4.10% = 1.25 percentage points × 100 = 125 basis points.

q: Which of these ratings is the LOWEST that still counts as investment grade?
o: BBB− from Standard & Poor's
BB+ from Standard & Poor's
Ba from Moody's
A− from Standard & Poor's
e: Investment grade covers the top four categories: BBB− or better at S&P and Baa or better at Moody's. BB+/Ba and below are high-yield (junk).

q:
Which risks does an investor holding U.S. Treasury notes face?
I. Interest rate risk
II. Reinvestment rate risk
III. Purchasing power risk
IV. Default risk
o: I and II only
IV only
I, II, III, and IV
I, II, and III only
e: Treasuries are default-risk free but not risk free: they still carry interest rate risk, reinvestment rate risk and purchasing power (inflation) risk.

q: Market rates drop two full percentage points, yet Dana's corporate bond, callable at $1,040, barely trades above $1,040. What best explains the muted price gain?
o: Wider bid-ask spreads from liquidity risk are holding the price down
Extension risk has lengthened the bond's expected life
Investors expect a call, so the price is capped near the call price
Lower rates raise purchasing power risk on the coupon
e: Call risk: issuers call after rates fall so they can refinance. Because buyers expect the call, the bond's price has limited room to rise above the call price, and the holder faces reinvestment at lower rates.

q: Marisol buys $50,000 par of a TIPS with a 2.0% coupon. The CPI rises 1.5% over the first six months. What is her first semiannual interest payment?
e: Adjusted principal = $50,000 × 1.015 = $50,750. Payment = $50,750 × (2.0% ÷ 2) = $50,750 × 1% = $507.50.

q: Theo bought a TIPS at its $1,000 par. This year the inflation adjustment raises the principal to $1,025, and he sells right afterward for $1,031. Ignoring coupon interest, how is the $31 above his cost treated?
o: $25 ordinary income; $6 capital gain
$0 ordinary income; $31 capital gain
$25 ordinary income; $31 capital gain
$31 ordinary income; $0 capital gain
e: The $25 principal increase is federal ordinary income for the year and raises basis to $1,025. Sale gain = $1,031 − $1,025 = $6.

q: Which of the following securities carries the direct backing and guarantee of the U.S. government?
o: Federal National Mortgage Association (FNMA) securities
Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corporation (FHLMC) securities
Student Loan Marketing Association (SLMA) securities
Government National Mortgage Association (GNMA) securities
e: Ginnie Mae (and the Farm Credit Administration) issues carry the direct U.S. guarantee. Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac and Sallie Mae have indirect backing and therefore slightly higher coupons.

q: Rates rise sharply and homeowners stop refinancing, so principal on Victor's mortgage pass-through comes back far more slowly than projected. Which risk is he experiencing?
o: Prepayment risk
Call risk
Extension risk
Event risk
e: Extension risk: when rates rise, prepayments slow, the pool's average life lengthens and expected principal is delayed, lowering the return.

q: Ruth, a cautious investor, wants the municipal bond with the least credit risk. Which should she choose?
o: A toll-bridge revenue bond
A city general obligation bond
An airport revenue bond
A private activity bond financing a sports stadium
e: GO bonds are backed by the issuer's taxing power (full faith and credit), often need voter approval and face debt limits, making them less risky than revenue or private activity bonds.

q: Owen faces a 35% marginal tax rate. A municipal bond yields 3.6%. What taxable equivalent yield must a corporate bond offer to match it?
e: TEY = tax-exempt yield ÷ (1 − marginal rate) = 3.6% ÷ 0.65 = 5.54%.

q: Priya pays a 32% federal and a 6% state income tax (add them for simplicity). Which bond gives her the highest after-tax yield?
o: A corporate bond yielding 6.5%
Her own state's municipal bond yielding 3.9%
A U.S. Treasury note yielding 5.2%
Another state's municipal bond yielding 4.4%
e: Out-of-state muni: federal exempt, state taxed: 4.4% × (1 − 0.06) = 4.14%. Corporate 6.5% × 0.62 = 4.03%; in-state muni 3.90%; Treasury 5.2% × 0.68 = 3.54%. Highest = 4.14%.

q: Ken bought a corporate bond, originally issued at par, for $900 in the secondary market. When he sells it for $960, accrued market discount is $40 and he never elected to include it annually. How is his $60 gain taxed?
o: $60 capital gain
$60 interest income
$40 interest income and $20 capital gain
$20 interest income and $40 capital gain
e: Market discount is generally deferred until sale and then treated as interest income. Only the gain in excess of accrued market discount is capital gain: $60 − $40 = $20.

q: For which client would a taxable zero-coupon corporate bond held in a regular brokerage account be the POOREST fit?
o: Parents who need a lump sum for tuition in six years
A retiree who needs monthly cash flow from the account
A pension fund matching a payout due in 12 years
A speculator expecting rates to fall who wants maximum price gain
e: Zeros pay nothing until maturity, yet taxable zeros create yearly phantom income. A retiree needing current cash flow gets no income and still owes tax.

q: A Canadian bank issues U.S.-dollar bonds that are sold and traded in the United States. What are these bonds called?
o: Yankee bonds
Eurodollar bonds
Eurobonds
Bulldog bonds
e: Yankee bonds are foreign-issuer bonds denominated in U.S. dollars and sold in the U.S., so U.S. investors avoid exchange rate risk.

q: A $1,000 par convertible bond has a conversion price of $80. The stock now trades at $96. What is the bond's conversion value?
e: Conversion ratio = $1,000 ÷ $80 = 12.5 shares. Conversion value = 12.5 × $96 = $1,200.

q: Using the facts shown, what is the bond's conversion premium as a percentage?
stem: Convertible bond (fictional): $1,000 par, conversion price $25, stock price $22.50, bond's market price $1,080, straight-bond (investment) value $960.
e: Conversion ratio = $1,000 ÷ $25 = 40; conversion value = 40 × $22.50 = $900. Conversion premium = ($1,080 − $900) ÷ $900 = $180 ÷ $900 = 20.00%.

q: Using the facts shown, what is the bond's investment premium as a percentage?
stem: Convertible bond (fictional): $1,000 par, conversion price $25, stock price $22.50, bond's market price $1,080, straight-bond (investment) value $960.
e: Investment premium = market price − investment value = $1,080 − $960 = $120. As a % of investment value: $120 ÷ $960 = 12.50%.

q: Using the facts shown, what is the bond's percentage downside risk?
stem: Convertible bond (fictional): $1,000 par, conversion price $25, stock price $22.50, bond's market price $1,080, straight-bond (investment) value $960.
e: Downside risk = (market price − investment value) ÷ market price = ($1,080 − $960) ÷ $1,080 = $120 ÷ $1,080 = 11.11%.

q: Using the facts shown, what is the bond's investment (straight-bond) value?
stem: Convertible bond (fictional): $1,000 par, 4% coupon paid semiannually, 10 years to maturity, comparable straight bonds yield 6%, conversion price $62.50, stock price $55.
e: Semiannual: N = 10 × 2 = 20, I/YR = 6 ÷ 2 = 3, PMT = $40 ÷ 2 = $20, FV = $1,000 → PV = $851.23.

q: Using the facts shown, what is the lowest price at which this convertible should trade?
stem: Convertible bond (fictional): $1,000 par, 4% coupon paid semiannually, 10 years to maturity, comparable straight bonds yield 6%, conversion price $62.50, stock price $55.
e: Ratio = $1,000 ÷ $62.50 = 16; conversion value = 16 × $55 = $880. Investment value = $851.23. Floor = greater of the two = $880.

q: Using the facts shown, suppose the convertible's market price is $1,000. What is its percentage downside risk?
stem: Convertible bond (fictional): $1,000 par, 4% coupon paid semiannually, 10 years to maturity, comparable straight bonds yield 6%, conversion price $62.50, stock price $55.
e: Downside risk = ($1,000 − $851.23) ÷ $1,000 = $148.77 ÷ $1,000 = 14.88%. (Investment value from N 20, I 3, PMT 20, FV 1,000.)

q: Lena's convertible bond has a conversion value of $1,150. The issuer announces it will call the bond at $1,040. What should she do?
o: Convert into stock before the call date
Accept the $1,040 call price
Keep the bond and keep collecting coupons
Insist on repayment at the $1,000 par value
e: This is a forced conversion: when conversion value exceeds the call price, the holder converts to receive the greater value ($1,150 vs $1,040). She can keep or sell the shares; interest payments end.

q: Which statement about convertible bonds is CORRECT?
o: They usually pay higher coupons than comparable straight bonds
The issuer decides when they convert under normal terms
Their prices are more volatile than the issuer's common stock
They usually pay lower coupons than comparable straight bonds
e: Convertibles trade a lower coupon for the right to convert. They are less volatile than the stock, usually issued by younger companies, and are good diversifiers (low correlation with straight bonds, moderate with stocks).

q: Grace will need a lump sum in exactly six years and wants it immunized against rate changes. Which single holding best does that?
o: A 6-year Treasury with a 7% coupon
A 4-year zero-coupon Treasury
A 6-year zero-coupon Treasury
A bond fund with a six-year average maturity
e: Immunization matches duration to the horizon. A zero's duration equals its maturity, so a six-year zero locks in the amount due in six years.

q: Why is an immunized bond portfolio not a 'set it and forget it' strategy?
o: Immunization only works while rates stay unchanged
Its duration falls faster than the liability's, so it must be rebalanced
Coupons must be spent rather than reinvested
Duration must be kept double the time horizon
e: Immunization offsets price risk against reinvestment risk when portfolio duration equals the horizon. Portfolio duration declines faster than the liability's, so periodic rebalancing is required.

q: Hector wants to lock in today's attractive long-term rates while keeping a large slice in short bonds, so he can redeploy cash if bond prices drop. Which structure fits?
o: A barbell
A bullet
A ladder
An immunized portfolio
e: A barbell holds only short- and long-term bonds: the long end locks in rates, the short end provides cash to use elsewhere. It needs active management as the short end matures.

q: Ivy needs a large sum in 10 years. She buys a 10-year bond now, an 8-year bond two years from now, and a 6-year bond four years from now. What strategy is this?
o: A ladder strategy
A barbell strategy
A rate anticipation swap
A bullet strategy
e: A bullet buys over time so everything matures together on the target date, matching duration to a single cash need and minimizing interest rate risk.

q: A bond manager expects interest rates to rise over the next year. Which swap is most consistent with that view?
o: Sell short-term bonds and buy long-term bonds
Sell a low-yield bond and buy a lower-quality, higher-yield bond
Sell long-term bonds and buy short-term bonds
Sell a government bond and buy a corporate bond
e: A rate anticipation swap shortens maturity when rates are expected to rise (less price sensitivity) and lengthens it when rates are expected to fall.

q: Jada sold bonds she bought for $10,000 for $8,600 after rates rose, and reinvested the proceeds in similar bonds. Using the textbook's simplified approach (loss × marginal rate) with a 24% rate, what tax saving does this tax swap create?
Without any interest rate forecast, a manager sells a 5-year A-rated bond yielding 4.6% and buys a 12-year BBB-rated bond yielding 5.4%. Which swap is this?
o: Pure yield pickup swap
Substitution swap
Rate anticipation swap
Tax swap
e: A pure yield pickup swap moves into a higher-YTM bond, typically by going longer and/or lower in quality, as here.

q: All else equal, which bond will show the greatest relative price change when market rates move?
o: 5-year maturity, 2% coupon, 3% YTM
20-year maturity, 7% coupon, 3% YTM
20-year maturity, 2% coupon, 8% YTM
20-year maturity, 2% coupon, 3% YTM
e: Relative price volatility rises with lower coupon, longer maturity and lower YTM. The 20-year, 2% coupon, 3% YTM bond has all three.

q: Jordan is aggressive and strongly expects interest rates to fall. Which bond portfolio best positions him to profit?
o: Short maturities with high coupons
Short maturities with low coupons
Long maturities with low coupons
Long maturities with high coupons
e: Expecting falling rates, build maximum rate sensitivity: long maturities and low coupons (high duration), to capture the largest capital gains.

q: Nadia lives in a state with a high income tax and wants taxable bonds with minimal default risk. Which is the best fit?
o: Federal National Mortgage Association (FNMA) debt
U.S. Treasury notes
High-yield corporate bonds
Investment-grade corporate bonds
e: Treasuries are default-risk free and their interest is excluded from state and local income tax, which matters most in high-tax states.

q: Walt and June, both 66, want inflation-adjusted cash each year of retirement with minimal default and call risk. Which approach does the textbook suggest?
o: A ladder of TIPS held in a traditional IRA
A barbell of T-bills and 30-year corporate bonds in a taxable account
A single 30-year zero-coupon corporate bond
High-yield bond funds held in a taxable account
e: A TIPS ladder supplies inflation-adjusted maturities each year; held to maturity it has no default, call or interest rate risk. In a traditional IRA, yearly inflation step-ups are not taxed currently.

q: An inverted yield curve most often appears when
o: the economy is in a strong, early expansion
the economy is peaking and no rate change is expected
investors demand a liquidity premium for long maturities
the Fed has tightened credit in an inflationary economy
e: An inverted curve appears when the Fed has tightened in an inflationary economy; it predicts falling rates and can signal a coming recession.

q: The 1-year Treasury rate is 3.0%, and 1-year rates are expected to be 3.4% next year and 3.9% the year after. Under the unbiased expectations theory, what should the 3-year rate be today?
Which yield curve theory can explain ONLY a normal, upward-sloping yield curve?
o: Unbiased expectations theory
Liquidity preference theory
Market segmentation theory
Efficient market hypothesis
e: Liquidity preference says investors need a premium to lend long, so the curve should always slope up; any other shape is a temporary aberration. The other two theories explain any shape.

q: A life insurer buys only long-term bonds to match its long-dated policy liabilities and will not move into shorter maturities even when they yield more. Which theory does this behavior support?
o: Market segmentation theory
Unbiased expectations theory
Liquidity preference theory
Rate anticipation theory
e: Market segmentation: institutions match assets to liabilities and stay in their preferred maturity segment, so supply and demand within each segment sets the curve's shape.

q: The yield curve is inverted: 1-year paper yields 5.2% and 20-year bonds yield 4.4%. Lucia, an income investor, expects the curve to return to normal. What does the textbook suggest?
o: Buy 1-year paper for its higher yield
Avoid bonds entirely until the curve flattens
Buy long-term bonds that are callable soon
Buy call-protected long-term bonds
e: When an inverted curve normalizes, short rates fall the most. Long bonds lock in high income and gain the most price; call protection keeps the issuer from redeeming them.

q: The curve is flat: 5-year and 30-year Treasuries both yield about 4.1%. Ben, an income investor, is thinking of moving from 5-year to 30-year bonds. What is the best advice?
o: Extend now, because the extra years add extra yield
Extend now, because long rates cannot rise when the curve is flat
Extend only if highly confident rates will fall soon
Extend now, because a flat curve predicts a rate decline
e: A flat curve means no pay for extra maturity risk. Income investors should buy long only if highly confident rates will drop; long rates could rise to restore a risk premium or with an overall rate increase.

q: Cobalt Corp. skipped its cumulative preferred dividends for the past two years. The board now wants to pay a common dividend. What must happen first?
o: Pay only the current year's preferred dividend
Pay all preferred arrears plus the current preferred dividend
Nothing; the skipped dividends are forfeited
File for bankruptcy over the missed dividends
e: With cumulative preferred, unpaid prior dividends (arrears) and the current preferred dividend must be paid before any common dividend.

q: A $50 par preferred stock pays a 5% dividend. Market yields on similar preferreds rise to 6.25%. What is its new intrinsic value, assuming no growth?
o: $50.00 (unchanged)
e: Dividend = 5% × $50 = $2.50. V = D ÷ r = $2.50 ÷ 0.0625 = $40.00, a 20% drop from $50.

q:
Which of the following are similarities between bonds and preferred stock?
I. Holders generally have no voting power
II. Holders rank ahead of common stockholders in bankruptcy
III. The issuer may deduct the payments
IV. A missed payment triggers bankruptcy
o: I, II, and III only
III and IV only
I, II, III, and IV
I and II only
e: Both carry no vote, have no share in profits, may be callable/convertible, may have sinking funds, and rank ahead of common. Preferred dividends are not deductible by the issuer, and missing one does not trigger bankruptcy.

q: Which statement about convertible preferred stock is CORRECT?
o: Its dividend is usually lower than the common dividend
Its conversion option loses value as the common stock rises
It is often used to finance venture capital and private equity firms
It ranks below common stock in a liquidation
e: Convertible preferred pays a higher dividend than common, ranks ahead of common, and lets holders share upside by converting. That upside makes it a common way to finance risky venture capital and private equity firms.

q: From the issuing corporation's point of view, which statement best describes raising capital with common stock instead of bonds?
o: It avoids fixed payments, but dividends are not tax-deductible
It avoids fixed payments, and dividends are tax-deductible
It requires fixed payments, but dividends are tax-deductible
It requires fixed payments, and interest is tax-deductible
e: Equity's corporate advantage is that it needs no fixed payments that could drain operating cash. Its corporate disadvantage is that dividends are not deductible, whereas bond interest is. Because stock lacks a fixed return, equity investors demand a higher expected return than bondholders.

q: Rafael, age 61, plans to retire in two years and fears a recession. He wants to add one stock whose results depend least on the business cycle. Which is the best fit?
o: A national automaker
A regional grocery chain
A casual-dining restaurant chain
An emerging robotics developer
e: Defensive stocks, such as grocery chains, sell everyday necessities, so demand holds up in recessions. They grow slowly but steadily and tend to gain favor in downturns, which fits Rafael's concern.

q: Brightway Corp. pays for a large expansion by issuing new bonds rather than new shares. Which risk to Brightway's stockholders increases most directly?
o: Market risk
Business risk
Financial risk
Interest rate risk
e: Financial risk is tied to how a firm acquires its assets. Choosing debt over equity adds leverage and raises financial risk for shareholders.

q: Lena pays $2 per share for warrants that let her buy 80 shares of Corvex at $25 per share any time in the next four years. Corvex rises to $31 and she exercises. Ignoring commissions, what is her profit?
e: Profit = (gain on stock − warrant cost) × shares. Gain per share = $31 − $25 = $6. Profit = ($6 − $2) × 80 = $320.

q: Which feature is typical of a warrant but NOT of a subscription right?
o: An exercise price below the stock's market price at issue
A life of only a few weeks before it expires
An offer to existing holders to keep their ownership share
An exercise price above the stock's market price at issue
e: Warrants are long-term, are usually priced above market when issued, and are typically attached as a sweetener to a bond or preferred issue. Rights are short-term, priced below market, and go to existing holders.

q: Which statement correctly contrasts a warrant with an exchange-listed call option?
o: The issuing company creates the warrant and customizes its terms
The warrant usually expires within nine months of issue
The warrant's terms are standardized by the Options Clearing Corporation
The warrant is written by an individual investor, not the company
e: A warrant is issued by the corporation with terms tailored to the issuer and buyer, and it usually runs several years. A listed call is written by an individual, has standardized OCC terms, and normally expires within nine months.

q: Which of the following defines the ex-dividend date?
o: The day the board of directors announces the dividend amount
The day the dividend is actually paid to shareholders
The first trading day on which a buyer does not get the declared dividend
The day the company's books are checked to list owners entitled to it
e: The ex-dividend date is the first day a security trades without the right to the already-declared dividend. A buyer must purchase before that date to be a shareholder of record.

q: Mateo wants to receive the next quarterly dividend on Halvern Corp. stock. Halvern's ex-dividend date is a Wednesday. Which purchase qualifies him for the dividend?
o: Buying on Wednesday at the market open
Buying on Wednesday just before the close
Buying on Thursday, the day after the ex-dividend date
Buying on Tuesday, the day before the ex-dividend date
e: To be a shareholder of record, an investor must buy before the ex-dividend date. A purchase on or after the ex-dividend date, at any time of day, does not qualify.

q: Tallis Inc. is worth $24 million and has 2 million shares outstanding. It declares a 20% stock dividend. What should the share price be afterward, all else equal?
e: Price before = $24,000,000 ÷ 2,000,000 = $12. Shares after = 2,000,000 × 1.20 = 2,400,000. Company value is theoretically unchanged, so price = $24,000,000 ÷ 2,400,000 = $10.

q: Priya owns 200 shares of Norland Co. that she bought at $45 each. The stock trades at $90 when Norland does a 3-for-2 split. Immediately afterward, what does she hold?
o: 300 shares at $60; basis $30 per share
300 shares at $60; basis $45 per share
400 shares at $45; basis $22.50 per share
300 shares at $90; basis $30 per share
e: 3-for-2 means 3 new shares for every 2 held: 200 × 3 ÷ 2 = 300 shares. Price = $90 × 2 ÷ 3 = $60 (value stays $18,000). Basis per share = $9,000 ÷ 300 = $30. A split is not taxable.

q: For a common-stock dividend to receive qualified (long-term capital gain) rates, how long must the shareholder have held the stock?
o: More than 12 months before the dividend payment date
At least 30 days in the 61-day window centered on the record date
More than 60 days in the 121-day window starting 60 days before the ex-dividend date
More than 60 days in the 121-day window starting on the record date
e: Qualified dividends must come from a domestic or qualified foreign corporation, and the stock must be held more than 60 days in the 121-day period that begins 60 days before the ex-dividend date (2026 edition figure). They are then taxed at 0%, 15% or 20% (2026 edition figure).

q: Hal has $1,200 of dividends reinvested through his employer's DRIP this year. What is the tax result?
o: No tax is due until he sells the shares bought with the dividends
Tax is due on the $1,200 now, but his basis does not change
No tax is due now, and his basis rises by $1,200
Tax is due on the $1,200 now, and his basis rises by $1,200
e: Dividends reinvested through a DRIP are taxed the same as cash dividends. Unlike cash dividends, the reinvested amount also increases the investor's tax basis.

q: Corin Corp. pays a 10% stock dividend, and shareholders have no option to take cash instead. What is the federal income tax result for a shareholder?
o: No tax now; existing basis is spread over more shares
Taxed now as a qualified dividend at the new shares' value
Taxed now as ordinary income at the new shares' value
No tax now; the new shares have a zero basis
e: A stock dividend is generally not taxable unless the holder could elect cash (constructive receipt). The shareholder's total basis stays the same and is spread over the larger number of shares, so basis per share falls.

q: The Aldergrove Fund holds securities worth $46.1 million and cash of $2.4 million, owes $1.3 million in liabilities, and has 2.36 million shares outstanding. What is its NAV per share?
e: NAV per share = (total assets − liabilities) ÷ shares. Assets = $46.1M + $2.4M = $48.5M. NAV = $48.5M − $1.3M = $47.2M. Per share = $47.2M ÷ 2.36M = $20.00.

q: Claire enters an order at 11:15 a.m. ET to buy shares of an open-end mutual fund. What price will she pay, before any sales load?
o: The NAV computed at the prior day's close
The NAV computed after that day's market close
The fund's NAV at the moment her order is entered
A market price set by supply and demand on an exchange
e: Mutual fund orders are filled at the next NAV calculated after the order is placed (forward pricing). Most funds calculate NAV after the 4:00 p.m. ET NYSE close.

q: Gwen, age 40, will put a large sum into one fund family and expects to hold it for more than 20 years. Which share class generally gives her the lowest total cost?
o: Class B shares with a contingent deferred sales charge
Class C shares with a level asset-based load
Whichever class has the smallest up-front charge
Class A shares with a front-end load
e: Class A shares charge the commission up front but generally have the lowest total cost structure, which makes them more suitable for long holding periods.

q: Teresa, an Oregon resident in a high tax bracket, wants bond fund income that is free of both federal and Oregon income tax. Which fund best fits?
o: An Oregon single-state municipal bond fund
A national municipal bond fund
A GNMA mortgage-backed securities fund
An investment-grade corporate bond fund
e: A single-state municipal fund holds bonds from one state, so residents of that state get income free of both federal and state tax (double tax exempt). Out-of-state residents usually avoid such funds because they can't use the state exemption.

q: Nolan, an Ohio resident, received $2,400 of interest from a national municipal bond fund. The fund reports that 15% of its interest came from Ohio issuers. How much of Nolan's interest is generally exempt from Ohio income tax?
e: A national muni fund's interest is free of federal tax, but most is subject to state tax. The portion from the investor's own state is generally state-exempt: $2,400 × 15% = $360.

q: What does a target-date (lifecycle) fund's glide path describe?
o: A fixed risk level the investor picks: conservative, moderate or growth
Moving up to 100% into stocks, bonds or cash based on forecasts
Its gradual shift from stocks toward bonds and cash as the target year nears
Holding about 60% stocks and 40% bonds at all times
e: A lifecycle (target-date) fund aims at a retirement year and becomes more conservative over time by cutting stocks and adding bonds and cash. That planned path is its glide path.

q: Which feature distinguishes a closed-end fund from an open-end mutual fund?
o: It continuously issues new shares to meet investor demand
Investors redeem their shares directly with the fund at NAV
Its share count rises and falls daily with purchases and redemptions
Its shares trade on an exchange and can sell above or below NAV
e: After its IPO a closed-end fund generally issues no new shares. Its shares trade like stock, so supply and demand can push the price to a premium or discount to NAV. They can also be bought on margin or sold short.

q: Which statement about unit investment trusts (UITs) is correct?
o: Unit holders are taxed each year on income and gains passed through
A board of directors oversees the trust's investment advisor
The portfolio is actively traded in response to market changes
The trust continues indefinitely, like a mutual fund
e: During the trust's term, interest, dividends and capital gains are passed through and taxed to unit holders, much like mutual fund shareholders. UITs are passively managed, have no board or advisor, and have a set life.

q: Marcus has $600,000 to invest. He wants a professional manager, wants to exclude tobacco stocks, and wants control over when gains are realized on each holding. Which vehicle best fits?
o: A large-cap index mutual fund
A separately managed account
A unit investment trust
A closed-end fund
e: In a separately managed account the investor owns 100% of the securities, can exclude specific investments, and keeps an individual cost basis in each position, which makes tax management easier. Minimums are often $50,000 or more.

q: Which feature mainly makes ETFs more tax-efficient than most actively managed mutual funds?
o: A legal exemption from distributing capital gains
They pay only qualified dividends
Lower turnover and in-kind redemptions
Forward pricing once at each day's close
e: Because they track indexes, ETFs have low turnover and so realize fewer gains. In an in-kind redemption the investor receives underlying securities instead of cash, so the transaction is not taxed.

q: Sofia wants low-cost, broad index exposure that she can trade during the day, buy on margin and sell short. Which investment best fits?
o: An S&P 500 index mutual fund
A stock unit investment trust
A hedge fund of funds
An S&P 500 index ETF
e: ETFs suit investors who want index or sector exposure at low cost, tax efficiency, and the ability to trade intraday, buy on margin and sell short.

q: Which client is the best candidate for a hedge fund investment?
o: Accredited, $8 million net worth, sophisticated, values manager skill
Age 26, $40,000 net worth, wants long-term growth
Retired widow, $300,000 net worth, needs monthly income
Couple saving for college in five years, $90,000 net worth
e: Hedge funds are private pools for wealthy, financially sophisticated (generally accredited) investors who care about managing loss risk and about the manager's skill. Smaller investors seeking growth or income are better served by mutual funds.

q: Which is a recognized drawback of a hedge fund of funds (FOF)?
o: It is open only to large institutions
A second layer of fees plus cash drag
Lower correlation with stocks than single hedge funds
All its assets sit in one hedge fund strategy
e: An FOF diversifies across about 10 to 30 hedge funds, but the extra management layer adds fees, and cash kept for withdrawals creates drag. Its returns have also been more correlated with stocks than those of single hedge funds.

q: The trustee of the Pellham Co. 401(k) plan is choosing a GIC for the plan's stable-value option and expects market interest rates to rise during the contract term. Which choice is most prudent?
o: A nonparticipating GIC
A nonparticipating GIC with a longer term
A participating GIC
A nonparticipating GIC with a shorter term
e: A participating GIC pays a variable return that follows interest rate changes, so it benefits if rates rise. A nonparticipating GIC pays a fixed rate and is the better choice when rates are expected to decline.

q: Jun invests $3,000 a month in a stock fund. Over four months the share prices are $20, $15, $24 and $16. What is his average cost per share?
e: Shares: 3,000/20 = 150; 3,000/15 = 200; 3,000/24 = 125; 3,000/16 = 187.5; total 662.5. Average cost = $12,000 ÷ 662.5 = $18.11. It is below the $18.75 average price because the fixed amount bought more shares at low prices.

q: Ava uses value averaging with a target of +$2,000 in account value each month. In month 1 she invests $2,000 at $25 per share. In month 2 the price is $20. How much must she invest in month 2?
e: Month 1: $2,000 ÷ $25 = 80 shares. Month 2 target value = $4,000. Current value = 80 × $20 = $1,600. Investment = $4,000 − $1,600 = $2,400 (buys 120 shares).

q: Under Owen's value averaging plan, his account should be worth $6,000 at the end of month 3. He holds 250 shares, and the price is now $27. What does the plan call for?
o: Buy $750 of shares
Invest the usual $2,000
Take no action until next month
Sell $750 of shares
e: Current value = 250 × $27 = $6,750, which is $750 above the $6,000 target. Unlike DCA, value averaging sells shares when the account exceeds its target, so Owen sells $750 of shares.

q: Imani buys 100 shares of a fund each quarter at prices of $40, $50 and $30. What are her total investment and average cost per share?
o: $12,000 invested; $40.00 per share
$12,000 invested; $38.30 per share
$15,000 invested; $50.00 per share
$9,000 invested; $30.00 per share
e: Cost = 100 × ($40 + $50 + $30) = $12,000 for 300 shares. Average cost = $12,000 ÷ 300 = $40.00, which equals the simple average price because the share count is the same each time.

q: Which investor is best suited to share averaging rather than dollar cost averaging?
o: A value investor who wants more shares when prices fall
A saver who needs the same dollar amount every month
A hands-on investor who will buy heavily to hit value targets
A momentum investor able to raise purchases as prices rise
e: Share averaging buys a fixed number of shares, so the investor commits more money as the price rises and less as it falls — the mirror image of DCA. It appeals to investors who can increase purchases and to momentum-style investors.

q: Which statement about dollar cost averaging is correct?
o: It works best in falling or fluctuating markets
It guarantees a profit if continued long enough
It beats a lump sum in a steadily rising market
It requires selling when the account is above target
e: DCA buys more shares when prices drop, lowering average cost, so it works best in declining or fluctuating markets. It does poorly in steadily rising markets and never guarantees a profit.

q: Dmitri bought shares of a fund in three lots: 200 at $10, 300 at $14 and 250 at $18. He now sells 200 shares at $20. Using the average cost method, what is his gain?
Rhea bought 500 fund shares for $9,750 plus a $250 commission. Later, $600 of taxable dividends were reinvested into 30 more shares. She now redeems all 530 shares at $23. What is her taxable gain?
e: Basis = $9,750 + $250 commission + $600 reinvested dividends = $10,600. Proceeds = 530 × $23 = $12,190. Gain = $12,190 − $10,600 = $1,590.

q: A fund's management fee is 0.55%, its 12b-1 fee is 0.25% and its other expenses are 0.15%. It also charges a 4% front-end load, and its trading commissions equal 0.10% of assets. What is its expense ratio?
e: Expense ratio = management fee + 12b-1 fee + other expenses = 0.55% + 0.25% + 0.15% = 0.95%. Loads and the fund's brokerage costs are excluded.

q: Last year a fund bought $120 million and sold $90 million of securities. Its average monthly assets were $300 million. What was its portfolio turnover?
e: Turnover = lesser of purchases or sales ÷ average monthly assets = $90M ÷ $300M = 30%.

q: Lucia puts $10,000 in each of two funds. Fund X gains 20% in year 1 and loses 10% in year 2. Fund Y gains 40% and then loses 25%. What are the ending values?
e: X: $10,000 × 1.20 × 0.90 = $10,800. Y: $10,000 × 1.40 × 0.75 = $10,500. The steadier fund ends ahead despite a lower best year — consistency matters.

q: A fund's NAV falls 40% in a bear market. What percentage gain does it need to get back to its starting value?
e: Required gain = loss ÷ (1 − loss) = 0.40 ÷ 0.60 = 66.67%. Check: $100 → $60; $60 × 1.6667 = $100.

q: Ava puts 30% of her portfolio in a fund she believes is 100% U.S. stocks. The manager has actually moved the fund to 75% stocks and 25% cash. What share of her total portfolio is really in stocks through this fund?
e: Effective stock exposure = 30% × 75% = 22.5%. Managers with flexibility to hold cash can push a client's real allocation away from plan, so check the prospectus.

q: In early December, Luis plans to invest $50,000 from a taxable account in a stock fund that had a strong year and is about to pay a large capital gain distribution. What is the best advice?
o: Buy now, since only long-time holders are taxed on distributions
Buy now, since reinvested distributions are not taxed
Check the distribution date and consider buying after it is paid
Buy Class C shares, which skip capital gain distributions
e: Buying a fund with large realized gains just before a distribution is essentially buying a tax liability, because the distribution is taxed no matter how briefly the buyer has held the fund. Checking the distribution date avoids this.

q: A fund family merges its worst-performing fund into a stronger fund, erasing the weak fund's record. What distortion in category return data does this create?
o: Survivorship bias that understates past category returns
Style drift that understates the category's risk
Forward pricing that inflates the surviving fund's NAV
Survivorship bias that overstates past category returns
e: When poor funds are merged away or closed, only stronger funds remain in the data, so the category's past returns look higher than they would if every fund were counted. This is survivorship bias.

q: Which statement about portfolio turnover and tax efficiency is correct?
o: High turnover always leads to large capital gain distributions
Funds pass their net realized capital losses through to shareholders
Low turnover doesn't guarantee tax efficiency if embedded gains are large
Trading costs from turnover are included in the expense ratio
e: A low-turnover manager has usually held stocks a long time, so large embedded gains can still be realized. High turnover can, but need not, create big distributions, because realized losses offset gains.

q: Which pairing of client objective and fund type follows this module's general suitability rules?
o: Maximum safety of principal → high-yield bond fund
Aggressive growth → U.S. government bond fund
High-bracket income seeker → corporate bond fund
Immediate liquidity → money market fund
e: General rules: growth → stock funds; income → bond funds; safety of principal → government bond funds; immediate liquidity → money market funds; high-bracket income → municipal bond funds.

q: Corinne is looking at a 15-year, $1,000 par bond with a 4% coupon paid semiannually. Comparable bonds now yield 5.5%. What is the bond's intrinsic value?
e: PV of semiannual coupons and par at the market yield. N = 30, I/YR = 5.5 (2 P/YR, so 2.75% per period), PMT = 40 ÷ 2 = 20, FV = 1,000 → PV = $848.13. Market rate above coupon, so a discount price is expected.

q: Ten-year, 6% semiannual-coupon bond; seven years remain until maturity. Comparable seven-year bonds yield 4.5%; ten-year bonds yield 5%. What should the bond sell for today?
e: Price the bond on its remaining life using the yield for that maturity: N = 14, I/YR = 4.5 (2 P/YR), PMT = 30, FV = 1,000 → PV = $1,089.22. The coupon exceeds the market yield, so it sells at a premium.

q: A callable bond is trading above par. Which ordering of its yields is correct, from highest to lowest?
o: YTC, YTM, current yield
YTM, current yield, YTC
All three are equal
Current yield, YTM, YTC
e: For a premium bond, current yield is highest; YTM is lower because it accounts for the premium shrinking to par; YTC is lowest because a call forces that loss sooner.

q:
Paolo owns a callable corporate bond priced at $1,080. Which statements are correct?
I. Its current yield is above its YTM.
II. Its YTC is below its YTM.
III. Its coupon rate is below current market yields for comparable bonds.
IV. Being called would give him the lowest of the three yields.
o: I and II only
I, II, and IV
III and IV only
I, II, III, and IV
e: A $1,080 price is a premium, so CY > YTM > YTC and a call is the worst case (I, II, IV). A premium means the coupon is above market yields, so III is false.

q: Hal bought a 4% coupon bond at par. Comparable bonds now yield 5%. If Hal sells today, what best describes the sale?
o: He sells above par because rates rose
He sells below par so the buyer earns about 5%
He sells at par; the coupon resets to 5%
He sells at par because the coupon is fixed
e: Bond prices and rates move inversely. The coupon stays at 4%, so the only way a buyer earns the new 5% market yield is to pay less than par.

q: Nadia's bond is priced at $980, has a duration of 6.2 (annual compounding), and the current YTM is 5%. If rates rise 75 basis points, what is the estimated new price using the textbook's duration formula?
e: ΔP/P = −D × [Δy ÷ (1 + y)] = −6.2 × (0.0075 ÷ 1.05) = −4.43%. −0.0443 × $980 = −$43.40, so the price falls to about $936.60.

q: A bond priced at $1,050 has a duration of 8.4 and a YTM of 6% (annual compounding). If rates fall 50 basis points, what is the approximate new price?
Using the textbook's semiannual-compounding convention, estimate the new price of a $1,000 bond with a duration of 5.0 and a 7% YTM if rates rise 1%.
e: Semiannual: halve the YTM in the denominator only. −5.0 × (0.01 ÷ 1.035) = −4.83%; $1,000 × (1 − 0.0483) ≈ $951.69.

q: A three-year, $1,000 bond pays a 6% annual coupon and yields 7%, so it is priced at $973.76. Using the cash-flow method, what is its duration?
o: 3.00 years
2.76 years
2.00 years
2.83 years

q: All else equal, which bond has the highest duration?
o: 20-year 6% coupon bond
20-year zero-coupon bond
10-year zero-coupon bond
20-year 8% coupon bond
e: Duration rises with maturity and falls as coupon rises. A zero's duration equals its maturity (20), longer than any coupon bond of that maturity.

q: Ms. Okafor will need the money in 9 years. All four AAA bonds below are available. Which best immunizes her against interest-rate risk?
o: Bond A: 9-year maturity, duration 7.2
Bond C: 15-year maturity, duration 10.6
Bond B: 12-year maturity, duration 9.1
Bond D: 10-year maturity, duration 8.0
e: Match duration, not maturity, to the time horizon. Bond B's 9.1-year duration is closest to her 9-year need.

q: An advisor strongly expects interest rates to drop over the next year. Which adjustment best positions a client's bond allocation?
o: Raise the portfolio's average duration
Move into short-term bond funds
Favor high-coupon, short-maturity bonds
Lower duration to match risk tolerance
e: When rates are expected to fall, higher-duration holdings deliver the largest price gains, so you lengthen duration. Shortening is the move when rates are expected to rise.

q: A short-term bond fund has a duration of 2.4 and yields 3.1%; a long-term fund has a duration of 12.9 and yields 4.4%. Using the rule of thumb, if rates jump 1%, about how many more percentage points would the long fund lose?
e: Rule of thumb: % change ≈ −duration × rate change. Short fund ≈ −2.4%; long fund ≈ −12.9%. Difference = 12.9 − 2.4 = 10.5 points — the extra risk taken for 1.3 points more yield.

q: A noncallable bond with positive convexity has a duration of 6. Rates rise 2.5%, so duration alone predicts a 15% price drop. What is the actual drop most likely to be?
o: Somewhat less than 15%
Exactly 15%
Somewhat more than 15%
About 2.5%
e: Duration assumes a straight line. With positive convexity, duration overstates losses when rates rise and understates gains when they fall, so the actual decline is smaller than 15%.

q: Rates are expected to fall sharply. Which holding is most likely to gain LESS than its duration predicts?
o: A noncallable Treasury bond
A long zero-coupon bond
A low-coupon noncallable bond
A callable corporate bond
e: Callable and mortgage-backed bonds have negative convexity: when rates fall they rise less than duration suggests, and when rates rise they fall more.

q: In the formula ΔP/P = −D × [Δy ÷ (1 + y)], what does y represent?
o: The bond's coupon rate
The bond's current yield to maturity
The bond's current yield
The expected change in rates
e: y is the current YTM (current market rate). The coupon is not needed because it is already reflected in the duration figure.

q: Which sequence describes top-down fundamental analysis?
o: Company, then industry, then economy
Economy, then industry, then company
Economy, then company, then industry
Price trends, then volume, then company
e: Top-down works from macro to micro: economic phase, then the industries expected to do best, then the best companies within them.

q: Brightwater Co. reports current assets of $450,000 (including $150,000 of inventory) and current liabilities of $300,000. What are its current ratio and quick ratio?
e: Current ratio = current assets ÷ current liabilities = 450,000 ÷ 300,000 = 1.5. Quick ratio = (450,000 − 150,000) ÷ 300,000 = 1.0.

q: Which is a core assumption of technical analysis?
o: Prices move in trends that persist over time
Only rational behavior drives security prices
Ratio analysis reveals a stock's true value
Prices instantly reflect all public news
e: Technicians assume supply and demand set prices, rational and irrational behavior both matter, and prices move in lasting trends because news reaches the market gradually.

q: The put-call ratio has spiked and mutual fund cash levels are unusually high. How would a contrarian read this?
o: Bearish, following the crowd
Bearish, since cash signals weakness
Bullish, since the crowd is bearish
Neutral; contrarians use only odd-lots
e: Contrarians do the opposite of the majority. Heavy put buying and high fund cash show bearish sentiment, so the contrarian turns bullish.

q: The gap between high-quality and lower-quality bond yields in the Barron's confidence index has narrowed. What does this indicate?
o: A flight to quality; a bearish sign
Rising default rates; a bearish sign
Nothing; it tracks only Treasuries
Investor confidence; a bullish sign
e: In confident markets investors sell high-grade bonds and buy lower-grade ones for yield (flight from quality), narrowing the spread. A widening spread is the bearish flight to quality.

q: A client is convinced markets are semistrong-form efficient. According to the textbook, which form of analysis could help him beat the market?
o: Technical analysis only
Neither technical nor fundamental
Fundamental analysis only
Both technical and fundamental
e: Technical analysis is of no help in any EMH form. Fundamental analysis can help only in the weak form, so under semistrong efficiency neither adds value.

q: Using fundamental analysis, an advisor concludes that Stock Q is undervalued after a steep drop. Which use of technical analysis does the textbook support?
o: Replace the valuation with chart signals
Sell because the trend is down
Wait for rising on-balance volume to buy
Ignore technicians; they cannot move prices
e: An MPT-minded advisor can use technical knowledge for execution timing, such as buying when on-balance volume starts rising or near support, since enough technicians act on these signals to move prices.

q: Halcyon Corp. has total assets of $800 million, liabilities of $300 million, net income of $60 million and dividends of $24 million. What is Halcyon's ROE?
e: Equity = assets − liabilities = $800M − $300M = $500M. ROE = net income ÷ equity = $60M ÷ $500M = 12.0%.

q: Using Halcyon's figures (ROE 12%, net income $60 million, dividends $24 million), what is its sustainable dividend growth rate?
e: Retention rate = ($60M − $24M) ÷ $60M = 0.60. g = ROE × RR = 0.12 × 0.60 = 7.2%.

q: Two firms each raise $40 million. Firm X uses all equity; Firm Y uses $15 million of equity and $25 million of debt. Each earns $4 million (ignore interest). What are their ROEs?
e: ROE = earnings ÷ equity. X: $4M ÷ $40M = 10.0%. Y: $4M ÷ $15M = 26.7%. Debt shrinks the equity base and magnifies ROE.

q: Juniper Inc. earns a steady 15% ROE. The board raises the dividend payout ratio from 30% to 60%. What happens to its sustainable growth rate?
o: Rises from 4.5% to 9.0%
Stays at 15.0%
Falls from 10.5% to 4.5%
Falls from 10.5% to 6.0%
e: g = ROE × retention. Before: 0.15 × 0.70 = 10.5%. After: 0.15 × 0.40 = 6.0%. Paying out more leaves less to reinvest, so growth slows.

q: Firm L has a 40% ROE, a 6% ROA and heavy long-term debt. Firm U has a 22% ROE, an 11% ROA and no debt. Which is likely to hold up better in a business contraction?
o: Firm L, because its ROE is higher
Firm U, with no fixed interest to pay
Firm L, because debt lifts its EPS
They should fare about the same
e: Leverage boosts ROE in good times, but fixed interest payments are hard to meet and debt is hard to pay down in a contraction. The unlevered firm carries no such burden.

q: A company's ROA is about one-seventh of its ROE. What does this most likely indicate?
o: The company has no debt
The company is heavily leveraged
The company pays no dividends
The company's assets are undervalued
e: A low ROA relative to ROE is a sign of high financial leverage: a small equity base makes modest asset returns look large to shareholders.

q: A preferred stock pays a fixed $4.25 annual dividend with no maturity. Ellen requires an 8.5% return. What is the most she should pay?
e: No-growth (perpetuity) model: V = D ÷ r = $4.25 ÷ 0.085 = $50.00. If quoted above $50, its yield is below 8.5% and it is overvalued for her.

q: Arbor Co. just paid a $1.80 dividend, expected to grow 5% a year indefinitely. An investor requires 11%. What is the stock's intrinsic value?
e: Constant growth model: D<sub>1</sub> = $1.80 × 1.05 = $1.89. V = $1.89 ÷ (0.11 − 0.05) = $31.50.

q: Selma is offered Kestrel stock at $54. It just paid $2.40, dividends should grow 4% a year, and she requires 9%. What should she conclude?
o: Undervalued; worth about $49.92
Overvalued; worth about $48.00
Overvalued; worth about $49.92
Undervalued; worth about $62.40
e: V = $2.40 × 1.04 ÷ (0.09 − 0.04) = $2.496 ÷ 0.05 = $49.92. Market price $54 exceeds intrinsic value, so the stock is overvalued and she should not buy at $54.

q: Wren Corp. just paid $1.40. Dividends should grow 8% a year for three years, then 3% indefinitely. The required return is 9%. Rounding each dividend to the cent, what is the intrinsic value?
Pinecrest LLC pays no dividends. Its free cash flow to equity was $2.50 per share this year and should grow 4% a year. A client requires 12%. What is the intrinsic value per share?
e: V = FCFE<sub>0</sub>(1 + g) ÷ (r − g) = $2.50 × 1.04 ÷ 0.08 = $2.60 ÷ 0.08 = $32.50.

q: Which model fits a profitable closely held company that has never paid a dividend and does not plan to?
o: Constant growth dividend discount model
No-growth dividend discount model
Discounted free cash flow model
Multistage dividend discount model
e: All three dividend discount models need dividends. With none expected, discount free cash flow to equity, the cash potentially available to pay dividends.

q:
Which statements about the constant growth dividend discount model are correct?
I. The growth rate must be lower than the required return.
II. A higher required return lowers the stock's value.
III. It is best suited to companies in the growth phase.
IV. Next year's dividend equals D0 × (1 + g).
o: I, II, and IV
I and III only
II and IV only
I, II, III, and IV
e: g must be below r (as g nears r, value explodes); raising r lowers value; D<sub>1</sub> = D<sub>0</sub>(1 + g). The Gordon model suits mature companies; the multistage model suits growth-phase firms, so III is false.

q: Larkspur stock trades at $63 with EPS of $4.20. The industry P/E is 18. Using the industry multiple, what is its estimated value, and what does it suggest?
o: $75.60; overvalued
$52.50; overvalued
$75.60; undervalued
$3.50; overvalued
e: Larkspur's P/E = $63 ÷ $4.20 = 15, below the industry's 18. Estimated value V = EPS × P/E = $4.20 × 18 = $75.60, above the $63 price, so it looks undervalued.

q: A client is choosing among four stocks. By the PEG ratio, which looks most attractive?
o: Cedar: P/E 12, growth 15%
Alder: P/E 24, growth 20%
Birch: P/E 15, growth 10%
Dogwood: P/E 10, growth 5%
e: PEG = P/E ÷ g (whole number). Alder 24 ÷ 20 = 1.20; Birch 15 ÷ 10 = 1.50; Cedar 12 ÷ 15 = 0.80; Dogwood 10 ÷ 5 = 2.00. Cedar is lowest and under 1.00.

q: A stock's earnings are expected to grow 6% and the investor requires 11%. Using the textbook formula, what is its price-to-free-cash-flow ratio?
e: P/FCF = (1 + g) ÷ (r − g) = 1.06 ÷ (0.11 − 0.06) = 1.06 ÷ 0.05 = 21.2.

q: Thistle stock trades at $42 with sales of $12 per share. Its peers average a P/S of 4.8. What is Thistle's P/S, and what does it suggest?
o: 3.5; possibly overvalued
3.5; possibly undervalued
0.29; possibly undervalued
4.8; fairly valued
e: P/S = price per share ÷ sales per share = $42 ÷ $12 = 3.5. Below the peer average of 4.8 suggests a possible value buy.

q: Which of these is a relative value method rather than an intrinsic value method?
o: Multistage dividend discount model
Price-to-earnings divided by growth
No-growth dividend discount model
Discounted free cash flow model
e: Relative (comparison) methods: P/E, PEG, P/FCF and P/S. Intrinsic (stand-alone) methods: the three dividend discount models and the discounted free cash flow model.

q: What is Harbor Point's annual net operating income (NOI)?
e: PGI = 12 × $1,500 × 12 + $4,000 = $220,000. Vacancy 5% = $11,000 → EGI $209,000. NOI = $209,000 − $74,000 = $135,000. Interest and depreciation are excluded because NOI measures the property's cash flow.
stem: Harbor Point (fictional): 12 units at $1,500/month each; parking income $4,000/yr; vacancy & collection losses 5% of PGI; cash operating expenses $74,000/yr; mortgage interest $38,000/yr; depreciation $20,000/yr.

q: What is the building's estimated value, and how does the asking price compare?
o: $1,200,000; the asking price is too high
$768,000; the asking price is too high
$1,200,000; the asking price is a bargain
$1,687,500; the asking price is a bargain
e: NOI = $135,000 − $39,000 = $96,000. Value = NOI ÷ cap rate = $96,000 ÷ 0.08 = $1,200,000. The $1,350,000 asking price exceeds intrinsic value, so a prudent buyer would not pay it.
stem: A small office building has effective gross income of $135,000 and cash operating expenses of $39,000. Comparable sales imply an 8% cap rate. The seller is asking $1,350,000.

q: Which pair of requirements allows a REIT to avoid federal income tax at the entity level?
o: Distribute at least 90% of net annual earnings; derive at least 75% of gross income from real estate
Distribute at least 75% of net annual earnings; derive at least 90% of gross income from real estate
Distribute all net annual earnings; derive all gross income from rents
Distribute at least 90% of net annual earnings; hold only mortgage loans
e: A REIT escapes entity-level federal income tax if it pays out at least 90% of net annual earnings and at least 75% of its gross income comes from real estate (2026 edition figures).

q: Grace, 58, wants real estate exposure in her taxable account. She has $15,000, may need the money on short notice, and wants diversification across property types. Which choice best fits?
o: The Z tranche of a collateralized mortgage obligation
A diversified, publicly traded equity REIT
A nonpublicly traded real estate limited partnership
A parcel of undeveloped land near a growing suburb
e: Publicly traded REITs let investors buy real estate exposure with modest sums, sell any number of shares on an exchange, and get diversification across properties and locations — the liquidity and marketability RELPs generally lack.

q:
Which of the following statements about RELPs and REITs are CORRECT?
I. Income a REIT shareholder receives is portfolio (investment) income, not passive income.
II. A RELP investor generally must sell the entire partnership interest rather than part of it.
III. A REIT is managed by a general partner.
IV. Losses from a REIT are restricted by the passive activity rules.
o: I and II only
II and IV only
III and IV only
I and III only
e: REIT shareholders receive investment income and REIT losses are capital losses not subject to passive activity limits (those limits apply to RELPs). A REIT is governed by a board; a RELP by a general partner, and RELP investors usually must sell the whole interest.

q: Lena wants to buy a CMO tranche but wants the least exposure to interest rate risk. Which tranche best fits?
o: A middle tranche, because risk is spread evenly
Tranche Z, because its interest accrues like a zero-coupon bond
Any tranche, because each gets a pro rata share of principal
Tranche A, because it receives all principal payments first
e: In a CMO, all tranches receive interest, but principal goes entirely to Tranche A until it is retired, then to B, and so on. Tranche A has the shortest repayment period and therefore the least interest rate risk; Tranche Z has the most.

q: Owen buys raw acreage, planning to sell once a highway extension is built. Which statement about his investment is CORRECT?
o: If the IRS treats him as a dealer, his gain on sale is ordinary income
Property taxes cannot be deducted until the land is sold
Appreciation is taxed each year as the land rises in value
The land produces positive cash flow from depreciation deductions
e: Undeveloped land is held purely for appreciation and has negative cash flow. Gains are recognized only on a taxable sale, as capital gain — unless the owner is treated as a real estate dealer, which makes the gain ordinary income. Risks include rezoning, permits, access and growth that never comes.

q: Rivet Corp. stock trades at $62. A Rivet $55 call trades for $9.40. What are the call's intrinsic value and time value per share?
o: Intrinsic $7.00; time value $16.40
Intrinsic $7.00; time value $2.40
Intrinsic $0; time value $9.40
Intrinsic $9.40; time value $0
e: Call intrinsic = max(0, $62 − $55) = $7.00. Time value = premium − intrinsic = $9.40 − $7.00 = $2.40.

q: Bexley stock trades at $48. Which option is in the money?
o: A $45 put
A $48 call
A $50 call
A $50 put
e: A put is in the money when the stock price is below the strike: $50 − $48 = $2 intrinsic value. Calls are in the money only when the stock is above the strike.

q: Dana writes one uncovered put with a $60 strike and receives a $4 premium. What is her maximum possible loss on the contract?
e: A put writer must buy at the strike. Worst case the stock goes to zero: loss = (strike − premium) × 100 = ($60 − $4) × 100 = $5,600. Her maximum gain is the $400 premium.

q: Marcus buys one put on Orrin Co. with a $40 strike for a $2.50 premium. What is his maximum possible gain on the contract?
o: Unlimited
e: A long put gains most if the stock falls to zero: (strike − premium) × 100 = ($40 − $2.50) × 100 = $3,750. Maximum loss is the $250 premium.

q: Under the Black-Scholes model, holding everything else constant, which change DECREASES the value of a call option?
o: Higher volatility of the stock's returns
A higher exercise price
A higher risk-free rate
A longer time until expiration
e: Stock price, time to expiration, volatility and the risk-free rate all move in the same direction as call value. The exercise price is the exception: a higher strike means the stock must rise further before the call has intrinsic value.

q: Which statement correctly contrasts the binomial and Black-Scholes option pricing models?
o: Black-Scholes ignores volatility; binomial is driven by volatility
Black-Scholes values American puts; binomial values only European calls
Binomial assumes continuous price change; Black-Scholes assumes discrete up-or-down moves
Binomial assumes discrete up-or-down price moves; Black-Scholes assumes continuous price change
e: The binomial (two-state) model steps the stock up or down in discrete increments; with many steps it approaches Black-Scholes, which assumes prices change continuously (geometric Brownian motion) and summarizes that through a volatility factor.

q: Hal buys one call with a $50 strike for a $3 premium and later exercises it, buying 100 shares. What is his cost basis in the shares?
e: When a call is exercised, the holder adds the premium to the basis of the stock purchased: ($50 + $3) × 100 = $5,300.

q: Priya wrote one call and received a $300 premium. The option expired unexercised. How is the $300 treated for tax?
o: Short-term capital gain on the expiration date
Ordinary income when the premium is received
No tax; the premium reduces the basis of her shares
Long-term capital gain if the call was open over one year
e: If an option expires, the writer reports the premium as a short-term capital gain on the expiration date, and the holder reports a capital loss on the same date.

q: Noor holds an American call with several months left. The call is in the money and she has decided to close the position. What is generally her better choice, and why?
o: Let the call expire, because in-the-money calls lose value if closed early
Exercise the call, because exercise captures both intrinsic and time value
Sell the call, because exercising early forfeits its time value
Exercise the call, because American options cannot be sold before expiration
e: Early exercise of an American option gives up its remaining time value. Selling it in the secondary market captures both intrinsic and time value — one reason pricing models are built on European options.

q: Ines owns 300 shares bought at $38. She writes 3 calls with a $45 strike for $1.80 each. At expiration the stock is $52 and the shares are called away. What is her total gain, ignoring costs?
e: Called away at $45: stock gain ($45 − $38) + premium $1.80 = $8.80 per share × 300 = $2,640. The covered call writer gives up all appreciation above the strike.

q: Arjun owns shares now worth $80 and buys a $75 put for $3 to protect them until expiration. What is the most he can lose per share from today's value through expiration?
e: The put lets him sell at $75 no matter how far the stock falls. Maximum loss = ($80 − $75) + $3 premium = $8 per share. Any rise above $80 is still his, less the $3 cost.

q: Theo writes one naked call on Calder Co. with an $85 strike for a $2.40 premium. The stock jumps to $97 and the call is exercised. What is Theo's net loss, ignoring costs?
e: He must buy at $97 to deliver at $85: loss $12 per share, less the $2.40 premium = $9.60 × 100 = $960. Because a stock has no price ceiling, naked call losses are theoretically unlimited.

q: Elise buys a $60 call for $3.50 and a $60 put for $2.75 on the same stock, same expiration. At expiration, outside what price range does she profit?
o: Below $53.75 or above $66.25
Below $56.50 or above $63.50
Below $57.25 or above $62.75
Between $53.75 and $66.25
e: A long straddle profits only if the stock moves by more than the total premiums paid: $3.50 + $2.75 = $6.25. Breakevens are $60 − $6.25 = $53.75 and $60 + $6.25 = $66.25.

q: Ruth, a retiree, holds a large blue-chip position that she expects to trade sideways for months. She wants extra income and would accept selling at a modestly higher price. Which strategy fits best?
o: Buy call options on the shares
Buy protective puts on the shares
Buy a long straddle on the shares
Write covered calls against the shares
e: Covered call writing is a conservative income strategy that works best in a sideways market: she keeps the premium, and the trade-off is giving up gains above the strike if the shares are called away.

q: Felix sold short 500 shares of a stock he expects to fall. He worries about a sudden surge. Which option position best limits his risk?
o: Write puts on the stock
Write calls on the stock
Buy calls on the stock
Buy puts on the stock
e: A short seller's risk is a price rise, which is theoretically unlimited. Buying calls offsets that: if the stock surges, the calls gain; if it falls, the calls expire and their cost trims the short-sale profit.

q: Beatrix holds a single stock with a large gain. She wants downside protection without spending cash on premiums and accepts capping her upside. Which strategy fits?
o: Write a put and write a call on the shares
Buy a put and write a call on the shares
Write a put and buy a call on the shares
Buy a put and buy a call on the shares
e: A zero-cost collar combines the long stock, a purchased put for protection, and a written call whose premium pays for the put. It protects a gain at little or no net cost, in exchange for giving up gains above the call strike.

q: All else equal, which set of conditions lets a call writer collect the LARGEST premium?
o: Stock price above the strike, stable stock, short time to expiration
Stock price below the strike, stable stock, long time to expiration
Stock price above the strike, volatile stock, long time to expiration
