Stock price below the strike, volatile stock, short time to expiration
e: Call premiums grow with (1) how far the stock sits above (or close to) the strike, (2) time remaining until expiration, and (3) the stock's volatility. An in-the-money call on a volatile stock with months to run earns the writer the most.

q: Walter's portfolio is mostly large-cap U.S. stock funds. He fears a broad market drop over the next few months but does not want to sell. Which hedge is most appropriate?
o: Buy call options on the S&P 500 Index
Buy puts on one stock in the largest fund
Write call options on the S&P 500 Index
Buy put options on the S&P 500 Index
e: Index puts act as portfolio insurance: losses in a large-cap portfolio are offset by gains on puts written on an index that matches it, such as the S&P 500. A portfolio with several asset classes may need several index options.

q: Corbin buys 2 corn futures contracts of 5,000 bushels each at $6.20 per bushel. The next day the price settles at $5.85. What happens to his account equity when it is marked to market?
o: No change until the contracts are closed
It falls by $1,750
It falls by $3,500
It rises by $3,500
e: Change = ($5.85 − $6.20) × 5,000 × 2 = −$0.35 × 10,000 = −$3,500. Daily marking to market moves the loss straight into his account equity.

q: An investor is long 2 stock index futures contracts at 4,210. Each contract has a $250 multiplier. At settlement the index is 4,198. What is the investor's result?
o: Gain of $6,000
Loss of $6,000
Loss of $24
Loss of $3,000
e: Points moved = 4,198 − 4,210 = −12. Result = −12 × $250 × 2 = −$6,000. Each index point is worth the multiplier per contract.

q: Initial margin on a futures position is $5,000 and maintenance margin is $3,600. After losses, Rosa's equity is $3,200. How much must she deposit?
e: When equity falls below maintenance margin, the account must be brought back to the initial margin: $5,000 − $3,200 = $1,800.

q: A juice bottler will need to buy large amounts of oranges next season and fears prices will rise. How should it hedge with futures?
o: Buy orange futures, a long hedge
Sell orange futures, a short hedge
No hedge; hedging is only needed when prices may fall
Sell orange futures, a long hedge
e: The bottler does not own the oranges it will need, so it is short the commodity. It buys futures (a long hedge): if prices rise, futures gains offset the higher cash-market cost.

q: Simone holds a large portfolio of long-term Treasury bonds. She expects interest rates to rise over the next quarter but wants to keep the bonds. Which futures position hedges her risk?
o: Sell stock index futures
Buy Treasury bond futures
Sell Treasury bond futures
Buy stock index futures
e: Rising rates push bond prices down. Selling bond futures creates a short position that gains as bond prices fall, offsetting losses on the bonds she holds.

q: Kofi held a futures contract for three months and had a $20,000 net gain at year end. How is the gain characterized for tax purposes?
o: $8,000 long-term and $12,000 short-term
$12,000 long-term and $8,000 short-term
$20,000 ordinary income
$20,000 short-term
e: Futures are marked to market at year end and net gains are treated as 60% long-term and 40% short-term (2026 edition figure): $20,000 × 60% = $12,000 LT; $20,000 × 40% = $8,000 ST.

q: Martina sells a rare coin collection held for nine years at a large gain. What is the maximum federal long-term capital gain rate on collectibles?
e: Long-term gains on collectibles (tangible assets other than real estate) face a maximum 28% rate (2026 edition figure), higher than the rate on long-term gains from securities.

q: In which environment is gold most likely to be attractive to investors?
o: Real interest rates are negative
Stock prices are rising steadily
Real interest rates are high
Inflation is falling and bond yields are rising
e: Gold pays no income, so its opportunity cost rises with real (after-inflation) interest rates. High real rates push investors toward bonds; negative real rates create a favorable environment for gold.

q: Harold, 70, has 40% of his net worth in rare stamps and needs more retirement income. What is the biggest planning concern with this allocation?
o: Stamps are highly correlated with his stock holdings
The stamps' basis will be stepped down at his death
Stamp income is taxed at ordinary income rates each year
He may be forced to sell into an illiquid market at a loss
e: Collectibles trade in inefficient, illiquid markets and produce only capital gains or losses. A retiree who needs income may have to sell them during a bear market for that asset class to buy income-producing financial assets.

q: What is a major tax advantage of investing in natural resource programs such as oil and gas limited partnerships?
o: Income is exempt from federal tax while held
Losses avoid capital loss limits by being treated as REIT losses
Pass-through of deductions such as depletion and intangible drilling costs
Gains are taxed at the 28% collectibles rate
e: Natural resource investments pass certain tax benefits to investors, notably depletion and intangible drilling cost deductions. Their risk is high, especially for exploratory drilling, but they have historically diversified stock and bond portfolios.

q: Which term describes the combined political and structural risks of investing in a particular nation, such as coups or confiscatory policies on dividends?
o: Country risk
Liquidity risk
Exchange rate risk
Reinvestment rate risk
e: Country risk is the composite of all risks of investing in a given country, including political events (revolutions, military coups) and structural ones (confiscatory treatment of profits, capital gains or dividends).

q: Isabel's portfolio is already filled with U.S. large-cap and small-cap funds. She wants to diversify away from U.S. companies. Which fund type fits best?
o: A U.S. large-cap index fund
An international fund
A global fund
A single-country fund
e: International funds hold only non-U.S. securities. Global funds include U.S. companies, so for an investor who already owns domestic funds they can duplicate existing holdings.

q: Which statement about American depositary receipts (ADRs) is CORRECT?
o: ADRs are illiquid because they trade only in the foreign market
Dividends are paid in dollars, but the holder still bears currency risk
ADRs are issued by the foreign company's home government
Currency risk is eliminated because ADRs trade in dollars
e: An ADR is a U.S. bank's trust receipt for foreign shares. It trades on U.S. exchanges and pays dividends in dollars, but the dividends are converted from the local currency and the price follows the home-market share, so exchange rate risk is not eliminated.

q: Which characteristic is LEAST typical of an emerging market?
o: Few, if any, restrictions on currency conversion
Strong prospects for economic growth
Low levels of equity capitalization
Lower regulatory standards and less transparency
e: Emerging markets often restrict currency conversion and foreign ownership, along with low capitalization, questionable liquidity, high volatility and weak transparency. Few conversion restrictions is a developed market trait.

q: What is her holding period return in U.S. dollars?
e: Cost = €5,000 ÷ 0.90 = $5,555.56. Proceeds = €5,400 ÷ 0.85 = $6,352.94. HPR = ($6,352.94 − $5,555.56) ÷ $5,555.56 = 14.35%. The dollar fell against the euro, boosting the dollar return.
stem: A U.S. investor buys shares of a eurozone company for €5,000 when $1 = €0.90. One year later she sells for €5,400 when $1 = €0.85.

q: What is his holding period return in U.S. dollars when the dollar strengthens to €0.95?
e: Cost = €5,000 ÷ 0.90 = $5,555.56. Proceeds = €5,400 ÷ 0.95 = $5,684.21. HPR = ($5,684.21 − $5,555.56) ÷ $5,555.56 = 2.32%. A rising dollar shrinks the dollar value of euro proceeds.
stem: A U.S. investor buys shares of a eurozone company for €5,000 when $1 = €0.90. One year later he sells for €5,400 when $1 = €0.95.

q: The quote is $1.10 per euro. Wendell converts $3,300 into euros before a trip. How many euros does he receive, ignoring fees?
e: Dollars per euro = 1.10, so euros per dollar = 1 ÷ 1.10 = 0.9091. $3,300 ÷ 1.10 = €3,000.

q: Hana, a Japanese investor, owns U.S. stocks. Holding stock prices constant, what currency move during the holding period helps her return measured in yen?
o: Neither, because her stocks are priced in dollars
The dollar weakens against the yen
The yen strengthens against the dollar
The yen weakens against the dollar
e: An investor holding foreign securities wants the home currency to fall against the foreign currency during the holding period. For a Japanese owner of U.S. stocks, a weaker yen (stronger dollar) converts sale proceeds into more yen.

q: What happens to a futures contract's price as the contract approaches expiration?
o: It moves away from the spot price as open interest falls
It converges toward the daily price limit
It converges toward the spot price, matching it at expiration
It locks at the initial margin level
e: The spot price is the current cash-market price. As expiration nears, a futures price approaches the spot price, and at expiration the two are the same.

q: The dollar currently buys 0.92 euros. If the U.S. dollar is revalued (strengthens), which quote could result?
o: $1 buys 0.89 euros
$1 still buys 0.92 euros, but euro goods cost more
One euro costs $1.12
$1 buys 0.95 euros
e: A stronger dollar buys more foreign currency per dollar, so euros per dollar rises (0.92 → 0.95) and it takes fewer dollars to buy one euro (1 ÷ 0.95 ≈ $1.053 versus $1.087).

q: Which statement best distinguishes asset allocation from diversification?
o: A portfolio can span several asset classes yet still be concentrated in one or two holdings per class.
Asset allocation and diversification are two names for the same portfolio process.
Diversification is only achieved once a portfolio holds all four broad asset classes.
Holding a dozen stocks in varied industries is asset allocation rather than diversification.
e: Allocation spreads money among classes (cash, fixed income, equities, real assets); diversification means holding enough loosely correlated securities to remove unsystematic risk. Allocation alone does not guarantee diversification, though a sound allocation usually includes enough securities in each class.

q: For CFP exam purposes, how many large-cap stocks in different industries does the textbook treat as enough for a diversified portfolio?
o: 4 to 7 stocks
25 to 30 stocks
10 to 15 stocks
About 100 stocks
e: Exam rule: 10–15 large-cap stocks across industries. Mid/small caps need more (25–30), and 4–7 mutual funds in different asset classes capture most of the benefit.

q: Dalia, 34, and her father Ramon, 67, are each considering the same aggressive growth fund whose annual returns swing widely. Why can Dalia hold it more safely?
o: Younger investors are not exposed to systematic risk.
Her longer horizon allows more time for strong years to offset weak ones.
The fund's standard deviation is lower for a younger shareholder.
Her portfolio beta automatically falls because of her age.
e: A longer time horizon is one of the two diversification levers the textbook names (with low correlation). The younger investor has more years for large positive returns to offset several negative ones.

q: A client is choosing between a Treasury bond fund expected to return 6% and a speculative overseas mining venture expected to return 8%. What is the best advice?
o: Pick the mining venture because its expected return is higher.
Pick the Treasury fund because lower risk is always the better choice.
Pick the mining venture because more risk guarantees a higher realized return.
Weigh the extra 2% against the much larger risk before choosing.
e: Risk and return must be evaluated together. The question is whether the additional expected return compensates for the additional risk; often it does not.

q: Which of the following is a systematic (nondiversifiable) risk?
o: Business risk
Financial risk
Marketability risk
Reinvestment rate risk
e: PRIME = Purchasing power, Reinvestment rate, Interest rate, Market, Exchange rate. These cannot be diversified away.

q:
Which of the following are unsystematic risks?
I. Default risk
II. Purchasing power risk
III. Investment manager risk
IV. Tax risk
o: I and III only
I, III, and IV only
II and IV only
I, II, III, and IV
e: Default, investment manager and tax risk are diversifiable (unsystematic). Purchasing power risk is systematic (PRIME).

q: Corwin owns common stock in a privately held regional bakery chain. Which risk does he NOT face as a shareholder?
o: Liquidity risk
Business risk
Default risk
Market risk
e: Default risk is a debt issuer failing to pay interest or principal. A corporation is not contractually bound to pay common dividends, so common stock has no default risk.

q: Priya, retired, wants a bond holding that eliminates reinvestment rate risk. Which should she consider?
o: A zero-coupon bond
A GNMA mortgage-backed security
A long-term coupon Treasury bond
A bond fund holding 20-year coupon bonds
e: Reinvestment rate risk arises when interim cash flows must be reinvested at lower rates. A zero-coupon bond makes no interim payments, so there is nothing to reinvest.

q: Theo, a U.S. investor, owns a Japanese bond that pays ¥10,000 of interest. When he bought it, $1 bought ¥100; today $1 buys ¥125. What happened to the dollar value of each interest payment?
o: The dollar strengthened; each payment is now worth $80, down $20.
The dollar weakened; each payment is now worth $125, up $25.
The dollar strengthened; each payment is now worth $125, up $25.
The dollar weakened; each payment is now worth $80, down $20.
e: Then: ¥10,000 ÷ 100 = $100. Now: ¥10,000 ÷ 125 = $80. A stronger dollar shrinks foreign-currency income for a U.S. investor (exchange rate risk); a weaker dollar helps.

q: Joanne keeps 80% of her long-term savings in CDs and money market funds "to be safe." Which risk is she most exposed to?
o: Business risk
Exchange rate risk
Purchasing power risk
Marketability risk
e: Cash equivalents manage liquidity but offer little principal growth, so unexpected inflation erodes their real value. Purchasing power risk mostly affects fixed-income holdings, CDs and cash.

q: The Harbor Growth Fund has a standard deviation of 24, the market index has a standard deviation of 15, and their correlation coefficient is 0.70. What is the fund's beta?
e: β = ρ × σ<sub>i</sub> ÷ σ<sub>m</sub> = 0.70 × 24 ÷ 15 = 1.12. Check: COV = 0.70 × 24 × 15 = 252; 252 ÷ 15<sup>2</sup> (225) = 1.12.

q: A stock's covariance with the market is 180, and the market's standard deviation is 15. What is the stock's beta?
e: β = COV<sub>im</sub> ÷ σ<sub>m</sub><sup>2</sup> = 180 ÷ (15 × 15 = 225) = 0.80.

q: Ana's $100,000 portfolio holds $50,000 of a stock with a beta of 1.40, $30,000 of a stock with a beta of 0.90, and $20,000 of a stock with a beta of 0.50. What is the portfolio's weighted beta?
Beta is the most appropriate measure of risk for which of the following?
o: A single, undiversified stock position
A well-diversified portfolio with little unsystematic risk
Any asset, whether or not it is diversified
An asset with a very low correlation to the market
e: Beta measures only systematic risk, so it is best used where unsystematic risk has been diversified away. Standard deviation is appropriate for any asset or portfolio.

q: A gold-mining fund has a standard deviation of 30 versus 15 for the S&P 500, yet its beta against the S&P 500 is only 0.40. Which conclusion is best?
o: The fund is 60% less volatile than the overall market.
The fund has less total risk than an S&P 500 index fund.
The low beta reflects low correlation with the index, not low volatility.
The fund's standard deviation figure must be misreported.
e: β = (σ<sub>i</sub> ÷ σ<sub>m</sub>) × ρ = (30 ÷ 15) × ρ = 0.40, so ρ = 0.20. As correlation falls, beta understates volatility and becomes less reliable; gold funds are the textbook's example.

q: Nadia has $60,000 in a large-cap fund that returned 11%, $25,000 in a bond fund that returned 6%, and $15,000 in a REIT that returned 4%. What was her portfolio's weighted average return?
A fund earned 12%, −4%, 9%, 15%, and 3% over the last five years. Using the textbook's convention for historical returns, what is its standard deviation?
e: Mean = 35 ÷ 5 = 7%. Squared deviations: 25, 121, 4, 64, 16 = 230. Sample variance = 230 ÷ (5 − 1) = 57.5. S = √57.5 = 7.58%. Calculator: enter each return with Σ+, read S<sub>x</sub>.

q: A portfolio has a mean annual return of 8% and a standard deviation of 6%. Assuming a normal distribution, within what range should returns fall about 95% of the time?
o: −10% to 26%
−4% to 20%
e: 95% ≈ mean ± 2 SD: 8% − 2(6%) = −4%; 8% + 2(6%) = 20%.

q: A stock fund has a mean return of 9% and a standard deviation of 5%. Assuming a normal distribution, about what share of annual returns would exceed 19%?
e: 19% = 9% + 2(5%), i.e., +2 SD. About 95% of returns fall within ±2 SD, leaving 5% outside, split evenly: 2.5% above 19% and 2.5% below −1%.

q: A fund's mean return is 10% with a standard deviation of 4%. Last year it returned 2%. What is that year's z-statistic?
o: −0.5
−8.0
−2.0
e: z = (value − mean) ÷ SD = (2 − 10) ÷ 4 = −2.0, i.e., two standard deviations below the mean.

q: When projecting the ending value of an unleveraged portfolio, which distribution does the textbook say to assume?
o: Normal
Platykurtic
Negatively skewed
Lognormal
e: An unleveraged portfolio's value can fall to zero but not below, while upside is unlimited, so terminal values follow a lognormal distribution with the mean above the median.

q: Which statement about return distributions is correct according to the textbook?
o: Kurtosis measures how asymmetric a distribution is around its mean.
Investors seeking to minimize volatility prefer a leptokurtic distribution.
In a positively skewed distribution, the median lies above the mean.
Semivariance measures deviations both above and below the mean.
e: A leptokurtic distribution is more peaked, with returns clustered near the mean, so volatility-averse investors prefer it. Skewness = asymmetry; semivariance = downside-only deviation.

q: An analyst is measuring risk from five years of a fund's historical returns. Which method does the textbook expect on the CFP exam?
o: Population standard deviation, dividing by n
Variance, dividing by n − 1 with no square root
Sample standard deviation, dividing by n − 1
Semivariance, using only below-mean returns
e: Historical returns are a sample, so S = √[Σ(r − mean)<sup>2</sup> ÷ (n − 1)] (calculator S<sub>x</sub>). The textbook expects only S to be computed on the exam.

q: A fund has an average annual return of 12%, a beta of 1.10, and a standard deviation of 18%. What is its coefficient of variation?
e: CV = σ ÷ mean return = 18 ÷ 12 = 1.50. Beta is extra data and is ignored.

q: Based on the data above, which fund offers the least total risk per unit of return?
o: Fund Q
Fund P
Fund R
Fund S
e: CV = σ ÷ mean. P: 12 ÷ 9 = 1.33; Q: 16 ÷ 14 = 1.14; R: 9 ÷ 6 = 1.50; S: 15 ÷ 11 = 1.36. Lowest CV wins, even though Q has the highest standard deviation.
stem:
FundMean returnStd. dev.
P9%12%
Q14%16%
R6%9%
S11%15%

q: A lower coefficient of variation indicates which of the following?
o: Less systematic risk per unit of return
A lower correlation with the market
Less total risk per unit of return
A higher expected return
e: CV = σ ÷ mean return: total risk per unit of return. When choosing, pick the lower CV.

q: Lena is choosing between a fund with a 7% mean return and 9% standard deviation and one with a 12% mean return and 14% standard deviation. Which tool best compares their risk per unit of return?
o: Covariance
Coefficient of variation
Beta
Coefficient of determination
e: When both returns and standard deviations differ, CV (σ ÷ mean) puts them on a common footing: 9 ÷ 7 = 1.29 vs. 14 ÷ 12 = 1.17, so the second fund carries less risk per unit of return.

q: Fund A has a standard deviation of 14, Fund B has a standard deviation of 20, and their correlation coefficient is 0.45. What is their covariance?
e: COV = ρ × σ<sub>A</sub> × σ<sub>B</sub> = 0.45 × 14 × 20 = 126.

q: Two funds have standard deviations of 12 and 16, and their covariance is 96. What is their correlation coefficient?
e: ρ = COV ÷ (σ<sub>i</sub> × σ<sub>j</sub>) = 96 ÷ (12 × 16 = 192) = 0.50.

q: A portfolio is 70% in a bond fund (standard deviation 12) and 30% in a stock fund (standard deviation 25). Their correlation is 0.20. What is the portfolio's standard deviation?
Under which condition does a two-asset portfolio's standard deviation equal the weighted average of the two assets' standard deviations?
o: The correlation coefficient is zero
The correlation coefficient is −1.0
The correlation coefficient is +1.0
The two assets are held in equal weights
e: Only with perfect positive correlation does no risk reduction occur. At any correlation below +1, the portfolio SD is less than the weighted average SD, so the full formula is needed.

q: Marcus already owns an S&P 500 index fund. Which additional fund would add the most diversification, based on each fund's correlation with the S&P 500?
o: Fund with a correlation of +0.36
Fund with a correlation of +0.93
Fund with a correlation of +0.85
Fund with a correlation of +0.70
e: The farther a correlation is below +1, the more diversification it adds. Low positive correlations diversify well; negative correlations are not required.

q: An investor puts 50% in each of two assets that both have a standard deviation of 15 and a correlation of −1.0. What is the portfolio's standard deviation?
e: 0.25(225) + 0.25(225) + 2(0.5)(0.5)(−1 × 15 × 15) = 56.25 + 56.25 − 112.5 = 0. With perfect negative correlation, equal SDs and a 50/50 split, risk is eliminated.

q: A fund's correlation coefficient with its benchmark is 0.80. What percentage of the fund's movement comes from unsystematic (non-benchmark) factors?
e: R<sup>2</sup> = 0.80<sup>2</sup> = 0.64, the share explained by the benchmark (systematic). Unsystematic = 1 − 0.64 = 0.36, or 36%.

q: A fund has a standard deviation of 20 and a covariance of 224 with the market, whose standard deviation is 16. What is the fund's R-squared, and is beta a reliable risk measure for it?
o: 0.70; yes, it meets the 0.70 threshold
0.49; no, it is below the 0.70 threshold
0.875; yes, beta is high enough to rely on
0.49; yes, any positive R-squared validates beta
e: ρ = 224 ÷ (20 × 16 = 320) = 0.70. R<sup>2</sup> = 0.70<sup>2</sup> = 0.49, below 0.70, so beta is unreliable; use standard-deviation measures (e.g., Sharpe) or a better-fitting benchmark.

q: A portfolio's R-squared with the S&P 500 is 0.45. Which performance measure is appropriate?
o: Treynor ratio
Jensen's alpha
Treynor and Jensen together
Sharpe ratio
e: Sharpe uses standard deviation (total risk), so it works at any R-squared and is required below 0.70. Treynor and Jensen use beta and assume a diversified portfolio.

q: An actively managed large-cap fund with materially higher expenses than an index fund shows an R-squared of 0.98 against the S&P 500. What is the best interpretation?
o: Its manager's stock picking explains 98% of its returns.
It is an excellent diversifier for an S&P 500 index fund.
Its beta is unreliable because R-squared is too high.
It behaves almost like an index fund while charging active fees.
e: An R-squared near 100% is expected of an index fund. An active fund with higher costs should not look this much like its benchmark; the client is paying active fees for index-like results.

q: Dana's investment produced a total return of 45% over six years. What is her simple (noncompounded) annual rate of return?
e: Simple rate of return = total return ÷ years held = 45% ÷ 6 = 7.5%. It is annualized but ignores compounding (time value of money).

q: A fund returned 10%, −5%, 18% and 7% in four consecutive years. Which pair correctly states its arithmetic mean and geometric mean?
o: Arithmetic 7.18%; geometric 7.50%
Arithmetic 10.00%; geometric 7.18%
Arithmetic 7.50%; geometric 7.18%
Arithmetic 7.50%; geometric 7.98%
e: AM = (10 − 5 + 18 + 7) ÷ 4 = 7.50%. GM: PV −1, FV = 1.10 × 0.95 × 1.18 × 1.07 = 1.3194, N 4 → I/YR = 7.18%. The GM is lower because returns varied.

q: Which statement about the arithmetic and geometric mean of a return series is CORRECT?
o: They are equal only when every period's return is the same.
The geometric mean exceeds the arithmetic mean when returns are volatile.
The arithmetic mean assumes each period's return is reinvested.
The geometric mean ignores the effect of compounding.
e: The geometric mean is always below the arithmetic mean except when all periodic returns are identical, because only the geometric mean reflects compounding.

q: Based on these facts, what is the time-weighted return on the stock?
e: TWR ignores Omar's second purchase and follows one share: CF0 = −40, CF1 = 2 (dividend), CF2 = 52. IRR = 16.54%.
stem: Omar buys one share of a stock for $40. At the end of Year 1 the stock pays a $2 dividend and Omar buys a second share for $46. At the end of Year 2 he sells both shares for $52 each. No dividend is paid in Year 2.

q: Based on these facts, what is Omar's dollar-weighted return?
e: DWR includes the investor's flows: CF0 = −40; CF1 = 2 − 46 = −44; CF2 = 2 × 52 = 104. IRR = 15.37%.
stem: Omar buys one share of a stock for $40. At the end of Year 1 the stock pays a $2 dividend and Omar buys a second share for $46. At the end of Year 2 he sells both shares for $52 each. No dividend is paid in Year 2.

q: Ben's account statement shows a lower return than the mutual fund's published return for the same period, even though he owned only that fund. What is the best explanation?
o: Published fund returns are dollar-weighted across all shareholders.
The fund reports a time-weighted return, which ignores the timing of Ben's deposits and withdrawals.
Time-weighted returns include investor contributions, so they always run higher.
The fund is quoting its SEC yield rather than any total return measure.
e: Managers cannot control shareholder flows, so funds report time-weighted returns. Ben's own result is dollar-weighted and reflects when he added or removed money, so the two usually differ.

q: Using the textbook's convention for annualizing a periodic IRR, what is Rosa's dollar-weighted return?
stem: Rosa invests $8,000 in a fund. It pays her a $120 cash dividend at the end of each quarter. When the fourth dividend is paid, her shares are worth $8,300.

q: A corporate bond has a 7% nominal return and inflation is 2.5%. Using the formula expected on the CFP exam, what is the real rate of return?
e: Real = [(1.07 ÷ 1.025) − 1] × 100 = 4.39%. Subtracting inflation (4.5%) is only an approximation.

q: Priya holds a 7% corporate bond, has a 30% combined federal and state marginal tax rate, and inflation is 2.5%. What is her after-tax, inflation-adjusted return?
e: After-tax = 7% × (1 − 0.30) = 4.9%. Real = [(1.049 ÷ 1.025) − 1] × 100 = 2.34%.

q: A credit card charges 1.5% interest per month, compounded monthly. What are the card's APR and effective annual rate?
Luis bought a bond for $960, collected $140 of interest, and sold it for $1,010. What is his holding period return?
Kendra earned an HPR of 20% on an investment she held for three years. Which statement is CORRECT?
o: The HPR overstates the investment's true annual return.
The HPR understates the investment's true annual return.
The HPR equals the investment's compound annual return.
The HPR already reflects when each cash flow occurred.
e: HPR ignores time. For holding periods longer than one year it overstates the annual return; for periods shorter than a year it understates it.

q: Based on these facts, what is the portfolio's Jensen's alpha?
o: −0.80%
e: Required (CAPM) return = 3% + 1.2(9% − 3%) = 10.2%. Alpha = 11% − 10.2% = +0.80%.
stem: A portfolio earned 11% with a beta of 1.2 and a standard deviation of 16%. The market returned 9% and the risk-free rate was 3%. Beta is reliable (R² = 0.85).

q: Based on these facts, what is the portfolio's Treynor ratio (in percentage points)?
e: Treynor = (r<sub>p</sub> − r<sub>f</sub>) ÷ β = (11 − 3) ÷ 1.2 = 6.67.
stem: A portfolio earned 11% with a beta of 1.2 and a standard deviation of 16%. The market returned 9% and the risk-free rate was 3%. Beta is reliable (R² = 0.85).

q: Based on these facts, what is the portfolio's Sharpe ratio?
e: Sharpe = (r<sub>p</sub> − r<sub>f</sub>) ÷ σ = (11 − 3) ÷ 16 = 0.50.
stem: A portfolio earned 11% with a beta of 1.2 and a standard deviation of 16%. The market returned 9% and the risk-free rate was 3%. Beta is reliable (R² = 0.85).

q: Which fund showed better risk-adjusted performance, and why?
o: Fund K, because it has the higher Sharpe ratio
Fund L, because it has the higher Treynor ratio
Fund L, because it has the higher Sharpe ratio
Fund K, because it has the higher Treynor ratio
e: R² is below 0.70, so beta is unreliable and the Sharpe ratio governs. Sharpe K = (10 − 3) ÷ 12 = 0.58; L = (13 − 3) ÷ 20 = 0.50. (Treynor would favor L: 9.09 vs. 7.78.)
stem: Risk-free rate 3%. Fund K: return 10%, standard deviation 12%, beta 0.9. Fund L: return 13%, standard deviation 20%, beta 1.1. Each fund's R² with the market is about 0.45.

q: A portfolio's Jensen's alpha is negative. Which statement must be true?
o: It earned less than the risk-free rate.
It has a beta below 1.0.
It plots below the security market line.
Its Sharpe ratio is below the market's.
e: Negative alpha means the actual return fell short of the CAPM required return for its beta, so it plots below the SML and the manager underperformed on a risk-adjusted basis.

q: Fund Q returned 9.5% with a tracking error of 3%. Fund R returned 10% with a tracking error of 6%. Their benchmark returned 8%. Which fund has the better information ratio?
o: Fund R, with an IR of 0.33
Fund R, with an IR of 1.67
Fund Q, with an IR of 3.17
Fund Q, with an IR of 0.50
e: IR = (R<sub>P</sub> − R<sub>B</sub>) ÷ tracking error. Q: (9.5 − 8) ÷ 3 = 0.50. R: (10 − 8) ÷ 6 = 0.33. Q's higher IR wins (0.50+ is often top quartile).

q: The information ratio becomes identical to the Sharpe ratio when
o: the benchmark is a constant-return, risk-free asset
the portfolio's beta equals 1.0
the tracking error equals zero
the benchmark is the S&P 500 Index
e: With a risk-free benchmark, the numerator becomes return minus the risk-free rate and the excess return's volatility is the portfolio's own standard deviation, which is the Sharpe ratio.

q: Which performance measure is an ABSOLUTE measure rather than a relative one?
o: Sharpe ratio
Treynor ratio
Jensen's alpha
Information ratio
e: Jensen's alpha states directly how much the return beat or missed its CAPM required return. Sharpe and Treynor are relative: they mean something only compared with another portfolio or a benchmark.

q: In a price-weighted index such as the DJIA, how does a $90 stock's influence compare with a $30 stock's, regardless of company size?
o: Three times as much
One-third as much
About the same
It depends on each firm's market capitalization
e: In a price-weighted index, influence is proportional to share price: $90 ÷ $30 = 3 times.

q: A company with a $45 billion market value belongs to a capitalization-weighted index whose members total $300 billion. What share of the index's price movement does it account for?
e: Cap weight = company value ÷ index value = $45B ÷ $300B = 15%.

q: Which of the following is NOT a shortcoming of the Dow Jones Industrial Average?
o: It ignores cash dividends.
It gives higher-priced stocks more influence.
It relies on a small sample of mostly blue-chip stocks.
It is poorly correlated with broader market indices.
e: Despite its flaws, the DJIA's correlation with the S&P 500 exceeds 0.95, so it still represents the market adequately. The other three are recognized weaknesses.

q: Marta manages a fund of developed-market stocks from Europe, Australasia and the Far East, excluding the U.S. and Canada. Which benchmark fits best?
o: Russell 2000 Index
MSCI EAFE Index
Wilshire 5000 Index
S&P 500 Index
e: MSCI EAFE is the most common benchmark for developed foreign markets in Europe, Australasia and the Far East, with no U.S. or Canadian stocks.

q: Which conclusion about the client's 7.9% return is most appropriate?
o: It lagged the S&P 500 by 2.1%, so the portfolio underperformed.
It beat a blended benchmark of 6.67%.
It beat a blended benchmark of 7.6%.
It beat the Russell 2000 by 1.9%, so the manager added value.
e: Blended benchmark = 0.50(10%) + 0.30(6%) + 0.20(4%) = 7.6%. At 7.9% the portfolio beat a benchmark that reflects how it is actually invested.
stem: A client's portfolio is 50% U.S. large-cap stock, 30% U.S. small-cap stock and 20% international developed stock. It returned 7.9% this year. The S&P 500 returned 10%, the Russell 2000 6%, and the MSCI EAFE 4%.

q: A bond with a 4.5% coupon is trading at $920. What is its current yield?
e: CY = annual interest ÷ market price = $45 ÷ $920 = 4.89%. It exceeds the coupon because the bond trades at a discount.

q: An 8-year bond with a 5% coupon paid semiannually is priced at $940. What is its yield to maturity?
e: 2 P/Yr, END: PV = −940, FV = 1,000, PMT = 25, N = 16 → I/YR = 5.95%.

q: Based on these facts, what is the bond's yield to call?
e: 2 P/Yr, END: PV = −1,080, FV = 1,020 (call price), PMT = 35, N = 8 → I/YR = 5.21%.
stem: A 10-year bond with a 7% semiannual coupon trades at $1,080. It is callable in 4 years at $1,020.

q: A 15-year bond with a 6% coupon trades at $930 and is callable at par in 5 years. Which ordering of its yields is expected?
o: Coupon > current yield > YTM > YTC
YTM > YTC > current yield > coupon
Current yield > YTC > YTM > coupon
YTC > YTM > current yield > coupon
e: For a discount bond, YTC is highest, then YTM, then current yield, with the coupon lowest. Here: YTC 7.71%, YTM 6.75%, CY 6.45%, coupon 6%.

q: A 10-year zero-coupon bond is priced at $600. Using the textbook's default conventions, what is its yield to maturity?
e: Zeros still use semiannual compounding: PV = −600, FV = 1,000, PMT = 0, N = 20, 2 P/Yr → I/YR = 5.17%.

q: Which assumption is built into a bond's yield to maturity?
o: Coupons are spent as received rather than reinvested.
Every coupon is reinvested at the YTM itself.
Coupons are reinvested at the bond's coupon rate.
The bond is redeemed at its first call date.
e: YTM is an IRR, so it assumes all coupons are reinvested at the calculated YTM. If rates fall, reinvested coupons earn less and the realized return falls short.

q: A municipal bond yields 3.6%. The investor's marginal federal rate is 35% and her state has no income tax. What is the bond's taxable equivalent yield?
e: TEY = tax-exempt yield ÷ (1 − marginal rate) = 3.6% ÷ 0.65 = 5.54%.

q: Using the textbook's method for a double tax-exempt bond, what is its taxable equivalent yield?
e: Itemizer: TEY = 3.4% ÷ [(1 − 0.06)(1 − 0.24)] = 3.4% ÷ 0.7144 = 4.76%.
stem: Grace itemizes deductions. Her marginal rates are 24% federal and 6% state. She is considering a 3.4% municipal bond issued by her own state, exempt from both federal and state income tax.

q: Felix can buy a 6% corporate bond or a 4.3% municipal bond of similar quality and maturity. His marginal federal rate is 32% and his state has no income tax. Based on yield alone, which should he prefer?
o: The corporate, because 6% beats the muni's stated 4.3%
The corporate, because the muni's TEY is only 2.92%
The municipal, because its TEY of 6.32% exceeds 6%
The municipal, because its TEY of 13.44% exceeds 6%
e: TEY = 4.3% ÷ (1 − 0.32) = 6.32% > 6%. Equivalently, the corporate's after-tax yield is 6% × 0.68 = 4.08% < 4.3%.

q: Which of the following is one of Markowitz's assumptions underlying modern portfolio theory?
o: Investors base decisions only on expected return and the variability of returns
Investors can borrow and lend unlimited sums at the risk-free rate
Investors measure portfolio risk with beta instead of standard deviation
Investor indifference strengthens the further they look past the holding period
e: MPT assumes mean-variance decision making: investors weigh only expected return and risk (standard deviation), prefer more return at a given risk, view each investment as a return distribution over a holding period, and maximize wealth over that period.

q: Based on these facts, which conclusion is correct?
o: The current portfolio is efficient because it can actually be built today
The current portfolio is inefficient; the proposed one cannot be built
The proposed portfolio dominates and should be implemented right away
Both portfolios are efficient because they carry the same risk level
e: At 12% standard deviation the best attainable return is 8%. The 6.5% portfolio lies below the frontier (attainable, dominated). The 10% claim lies above the frontier, outside the set of possible portfolios.
stem: An optimizer shows that, for the available asset classes, the efficient frontier offers a maximum expected return of 8% at a 12% standard deviation. The client's current portfolio: 6.5% expected return, 12% standard deviation. A product pitch claims a portfolio from the same asset classes with 10% expected return at 12% standard deviation.

q: Compared with a moderately risk-tolerant investor, a highly risk-averse investor's indifference curves are
o: flatter, touching the efficient frontier at a lower-risk point
steeper, touching the efficient frontier at a higher-risk point
steeper, touching the efficient frontier at a lower-risk point
downward sloping, since added risk lowers the return demanded
e: The more risk averse the investor, the more extra return is demanded per unit of risk, so the curve is steeper and its tangency with the frontier lies to the left, at a lower-risk portfolio.

q: Investor A's indifference curve is tangent to the efficient frontier at a portfolio with a 10% standard deviation; Investor B's is tangent at 18%. Which statement is most accurate?
o: B has steeper indifference curves and is more risk averse than A
A's portfolio is inefficient because it has a lower expected return
No conclusion about risk attitudes can be drawn from tangency points
B has flatter indifference curves and is more risk tolerant than A
e: A tangency farther right (higher risk) reflects a flatter indifference curve: the investor needs only a small extra return to accept more risk, so B is more risk tolerant. Both portfolios are efficient.

q: Dana owns 14 mutual funds. Nine are large-cap U.S. stock funds whose top-10 holdings largely repeat. Under MPT principles, what is the best observation?
o: The overlap mimics a costly index fund without adding diversification
More funds always reduce unsystematic risk, so she should add more
She holds too few securities to eliminate unsystematic risk
Overlap lowers her correlation with bonds, which reduces total risk
e: Owning many funds with the same top holdings (overlap) creates a de facto index fund with extra cost. A handful of concentrated funds, or one large balanced fund, can remove most unsystematic risk.

q: A portfolio has risen in value since it was built, and the advisor has new cash to invest. Under the textbook's correlation guidance, which addition would most likely lower portfolio standard deviation?
o: The portfolio's best performer, to add to existing momentum
A recent decliner that is negatively correlated with the portfolio
A fund highly correlated with current holdings, for consistency
Whichever available security has the highest standard deviation
e: The correlation coefficient is the key to cutting portfolio risk. A security that has dropped while the portfolio rose shows negative correlation with it, so adding it helps lower overall standard deviation.

q: A stock has a beta of 1.4. The T-bill yields 3.5%, and the market is expected to return 9.5%. What is the stock's required return under CAPM?
e: r = r<sub>f</sub> + (r<sub>m</sub> − r<sub>f</sub>)β = 3.5% + (9.5% − 3.5%) × 1.4 = 3.5% + 8.4% = 11.9%.

q: The market is expected to return 8.5% and T-bills yield 2.5%. For a stock with a beta of 0.7, what are the market risk premium and the stock risk premium?
o: Market risk premium 8.5%; stock risk premium 5.95%
Market risk premium 6.0%; stock risk premium 6.7%
Market risk premium 4.2%; stock risk premium 6.0%
Market risk premium 6.0%; stock risk premium 4.2%
e: Market risk premium = r<sub>m</sub> − r<sub>f</sub> = 8.5% − 2.5% = 6.0%. Stock risk premium = (r<sub>m</sub> − r<sub>f</sub>) × β = 6.0% × 0.7 = 4.2%.

q: Based on CAPM, what is the best recommendation for Priya?
o: Pass: CAPM expects 10.5%, below her 12% required return
Buy: CAPM expects 14.25%, above her 12% required return
Pass: CAPM expects 7.5%, below her 12% required return
Buy: a beta above 1.0 ensures it will beat her 12% target
e: CAPM expected return = 3% + (9% − 3%) × 1.25 = 3% + 7.5% = 10.5%. Because 10.5% is below her 12% required return, the fund should be rejected.
stem: Priya requires a 12% return from a new holding. The fund she is considering has a beta of 1.25. The market is expected to return 9%, and T-bills yield 3%.

q: An asset has a beta of −0.4. The risk-free rate is 4% and the market is expected to return 11%. What is its CAPM required return?
o: −2.80%
−0.40%
e: r = 4% + (11% − 4%) × (−0.4) = 4% − 2.8% = 1.2%. Negative-beta assets move against the market; investors accept a low return for their diversification value.

q: Using CAPM, which conclusion about Stocks Q and R is correct?
o: Q plots below the SML (sell); R plots above the SML (buy)
Both plot on the SML because both forecasts exceed the risk-free rate
Q plots above the SML (buy); R plots below the SML (sell or short)
R is the better buy because its forecast return is the higher one
e: Required: Q = 4% + 6% × 0.9 = 9.4%; R = 4% + 6% × 1.6 = 13.6%. Q's 10% forecast exceeds 9.4% (undervalued, above SML); R's 12.5% is below 13.6% (overvalued, below SML).
stem:
Risk-free rate 4%; expected market return 10%.
Stock Q: beta 0.9, analyst forecast return 10.0%
Stock R: beta 1.6, analyst forecast return 12.5%

q: The risk-free rate is 3%. The market portfolio is expected to return 10% with a 16% standard deviation. Using the CML, what is the expected return of an efficient portfolio with a 12% standard deviation?
e: r<sub>p</sub> = r<sub>f</sub> + σ<sub>p</sub> × [(r<sub>m</sub> − r<sub>f</sub>) ÷ σ<sub>m</sub>] = 3% + 12% × (7% ÷ 16%) = 3% + 5.25% = 8.25%.

q: Expected inflation rises and the risk-free rate moves from 3.0% to 4.5%; the market risk premium stays at 6%. What happens to the required return on a stock with a beta of 1.2?
o: It rises from 10.2% to 11.7% as the SML shifts up in parallel
It rises from 10.2% to 12.0% as the SML becomes steeper
It stays at 10.2% because inflation changes only the slope
It falls to 8.7% because higher rates cut required returns
e: Before: 3% + 6% × 1.2 = 10.2%. After: 4.5% + 6% × 1.2 = 11.7%. Inflation moves the risk-free rate, producing a parallel shift that raises all required returns by 1.5 points.

q: Investors in general become more risk averse, while the risk-free rate is unchanged. What happens to the SML?
o: It shifts upward, parallel to the original line
It pivots at the risk-free rate and becomes steeper
It pivots at the risk-free rate and becomes flatter
Its intercept falls while its slope is unchanged
e: More risk aversion raises the market risk premium (the price of risk), which steepens the SML around the unchanged risk-free intercept. Only risky assets are affected.

q: Using APT, what is the expected return on this stock?
stem:
Risk-free return: 2.5%.
Unanticipated inflation: sensitivity 1.2, risk premium 4%
Industrial production (GDP): sensitivity 0.6, risk premium 5%
Interest rates (yield curve): sensitivity 0.5, risk premium 3%

q: Which of the following is NOT one of the four primary APT factors identified in the textbook?
o: Inflation
Industrial production (changes in GDP)
The yield curve (interest rates)
Stock market trading volume
e: The four primary APT factors are inflation, industrial production (GDP), risk premiums, and the yield curve. Only unexpected changes in them matter; trading volume is not among them.

q: Which of the following is one of the assumptions Sharpe stipulated for CAPM?
o: Capital markets are always in equilibrium, so assets are properly priced
Investors hold differing expectations about each asset's return distribution
Taxes and transaction costs are central to every investment decision
Investors can borrow only at rates well above the risk-free rate
e: CAPM assumes identical expectations, borrowing and lending at the risk-free rate (e.g., 13-week T-bill), no taxes or transaction costs, and markets that are always in equilibrium with every asset properly priced.

q: Under the semistrong form of the efficient market hypothesis, which approach could still produce above-market returns?
o: Fundamental analysis of financial statements
Trading on material inside information
Charting support and resistance levels
Buying right after favorable earnings news
e: The semistrong form holds that prices reflect all public information (historical data, financial statements, industry and economic outlook). Only inside information could beat the market.

q: Which statements are correct?
o: I and II only
I, III, and IV
II and III only
III only
e: Marcus uses fundamental analysis, which can add value only under the weak form (I true). Elena's technical rules are rejected by every form (II false, IV true). Theo's passive indexing fits the semistrong and strong forms (III true).
stem:
Marcus studies annual reports to find mispriced stocks. Elena trades on moving-average crossovers. Theo buys a total-market index fund and holds it.

I. Marcus's approach is consistent with the weak form of the EMH.
II. Elena's approach is supported by the weak form of the EMH.
III. Theo's approach is consistent with the semistrong and strong forms.
IV. No form of the EMH supports Elena's approach.

q: Which type of research has tended to SUPPORT the semistrong form of the EMH?
o: Return-prediction studies of January and weekend effects
Cross-sectional studies showing low-P/E stocks outperform
Studies showing insiders earn abnormal trading profits
Event studies of splits, IPOs, and surprise announcements
e: Event studies found prices adjust quickly to stock splits, IPOs, exchange listings, and surprise news, confirming semistrong efficiency. Return-prediction and cross-sectional studies found anomalies.

q: Jonah buys small-company stocks each December and sells them in January. Which anomaly is he using, and what caveat applies?
o: January effect; it now tends to show up earlier, in December
Weekend effect; price moves may not cover transaction costs
Neglected-firm effect; it may just be an extension of the size effect
Dividend-yield anomaly; higher-yielding stocks tend to outperform
e: The January effect seeks lower December prices (partly from tax selling) and higher January prices. Because it is widely known, it has shifted earlier into December, so treating it as a fixed rule is risky.

q: In a semistrong-form test, CAPM sets a stock's required return at 9%. Over the period, the stock actually returns 12.5%. What abnormal return do researchers attribute to it?
o: −3.5%
e: Abnormal return = actual return − CAPM required return = 12.5% − 9% = 3.5%. Persistent abnormal returns from public information would contradict semistrong efficiency.

q: A client believes U.S. large-cap stocks are highly efficient but emerging markets are not. Which implementation best fits that view?
o: Use an active manager for large caps and index emerging markets
Use active managers everywhere, since some segments are inefficient
Index the large-cap sleeve and use an active manager for emerging markets
Avoid emerging markets entirely because their statements are unreliable
e: Different parts of the market have different degrees of efficiency. Large caps tend to be efficient (index them); emerging markets are less efficient, so an active manager may find opportunities there.

q: According to the textbook, why have low-P/E and high book-to-market stocks tended to deliver higher returns?
o: They are fundamentally strong firms with highly predictable earnings growth
They carry lower betas, and CAPM rewards low beta with higher returns
Securities laws restrict insiders from trading them, reducing competition
They're shunned as weak firms and assigned high required returns
e: Low-P/E and high-BV/MV companies often look weak, so most analysts ignore them. Investors assign them high required returns for perceived risk; as fortunes improve, value investors realize those returns.

q: According to the Brinson, Hood, and Beebower study, what explains more than 90% of the variability of a portfolio's returns?
o: Asset allocation
Security selection
Market timing
Expense ratios
e: The widely quoted (and later debated) Brinson study found that more than 90% of the variability of portfolio returns is driven by the asset allocation decision, with selection and timing contributing little.

q: A prospect wants to hire only managers who consistently rank in the top 25% of their asset class. What does the textbook suggest?
o: Most active funds beat their indexes, so this is easy to accomplish
Rare; strong stretches are usually followed by subpar ones
Top-quartile consistency is common among large-cap growth funds
A past top-quartile ranking virtually ensures future outperformance
e: Even excellent long-record managers tend to have periods of strong performance followed by subpar periods (regression to the mean). Staying consistently in the top 25% of an asset class is rare.

q: A client wants to keep $60,000 available for a home down payment in three years. In which IPS content area should this be recorded?
o: Return requirement
Laws and regulations
Liquidity
Permitted and excluded investments
e: The liquidity section captures cash needs such as an emergency fund or an amount needed within three to five years for a planned expenditure. Many advisors keep such money out of stocks.

q: How should Walter's IPS describe his risk tolerance?
o: Low ability and low willingness to take risk
High ability and high willingness, since wealth sets tolerance
Low ability but high willingness to take risk
High ability but low willingness to take risk
e: Ability reflects resources and circumstances; willingness reflects emotional comfort with volatility. Walter has ample resources (high ability) but dislikes swings (low willingness), and may not need much risk.
stem: Walter, 61, has $4 million invested, is in excellent health, is fully insured, and has a pension that covers his living expenses. He checks his balances daily and is upset by any decline.

q: An IPS targets a 4.5% real return, and the advisor assumes 2.5% average inflation. Using the textbook's simple approach, what nominal return requirement should the IPS state?
e: Simple method: return requirement = target real return + average inflation = 4.5% + 2.5% = 7.0%. The IPS could also say returns should beat inflation by 4.5% on average.

q: Research shows that the pain of a loss outweighs the pleasure of an equal gain. Which concept, introduced by Kahneman and Tversky, does this describe?
o: Risk aversion
Loss aversion
Overconfidence
Representativeness
e: Loss aversion: losses hurt more than equal gains please, so investors may gamble to avoid a sure loss or hold losers hoping to break even. Kahneman and Tversky first introduced it.

q: An advisor runs a Monte Carlo retirement projection using the returns of the Wilshire 5000, but the client's funds carry meaningful fees. What is the main risk?
o: It will understate success because it ignores the market's positive bias
Monte Carlo cannot model withdrawals, so the result is meaningless
The projection may overstate future values and sustainable withdrawals
Fees matter only in taxable accounts, so there is no distortion
e: A known weakness of Monte Carlo is simulating asset-class index returns rather than the actual fee-bearing holdings. That can significantly overstate future value or how long distributions can last.

q: A client expects the Fed to keep raising rates over the next year and wants to stay flexible. Which holding best fits the textbook's guidance?
o: A long-term investment-grade corporate bond fund
Shares of a highly leveraged electric utility
A 20-year zero-coupon Treasury bond
Money market funds or short-term Treasury bills
e: Liquid and short-term holdings (money market funds, T-bills and notes) let an investor reinvest at higher yields as rates continue to rise, avoiding the price losses of long-duration assets.

q: As an economy begins recovering from a recession, which pattern does the textbook describe?
o: Unemployment falls, income grows, and cyclicals begin to rise
Consumer noncyclicals lead as investors seek steady, reliable demand
Basic materials and energy lead on renewed inflation fears
Utilities rally because interest rates are climbing quickly
e: In recovery, unemployment declines and personal income grows, so cyclical stocks begin to move; autos may keep benefiting from low-cost financing.

q: Inflation is accelerating sharply. Which holding is most likely to hold up, according to the textbook?
o: A long-term Treasury bond
Shares of an oil and gas producer
An intermediate-term corporate bond fund
A heavily indebted bank stock
e: Strong inflation hurts stocks in most industries and bonds generally, but commodity-linked areas (energy producers, natural resources, real estate) may see their share prices climb.

q: Which statement best describes sensitivity analysis?
o: Running thousands of random trials to build a probability distribution
Measuring a stock's volatility relative to the overall market
Testing NPV and IRR under pessimistic, expected and optimistic inputs
Shifting among industries as the business cycle progresses
e: Sensitivity analysis changes one input at a time under pessimistic, expected, and optimistic assumptions and reviews the effect on NPV and IRR, revealing how reliable an investment's outcome is.

q: Which statement about tactical asset allocation (TAA) is correct?
o: It holds a fixed mix until a major life event calls for a change
It usually has lower turnover and lower costs than strategic allocation
It is generally preferred by passive, buy-and-hold investors
A contrarian, market-timing approach that buys out-of-favor classes
e: TAA continually shifts the mix to exploit perceived mispricing, gives little weight to long-term goals, is inherently contrarian, and costs more to run than strategic allocation.

q: A lifecycle (target-date) 401(k) fund gradually shifts toward bonds as participants age, regardless of market conditions. This is an example of
o: rebalancing under a strategic asset allocation
tactical asset allocation based on market timing
sector rotation across the business cycle
a core-and-satellite investment strategy
e: Lifecycle funds adjust allocation for age and risk tolerance, not market timing; the textbook cites them as rebalancing within a strategic asset allocation orientation.

q: A $500,000 portfolio has a strategic target of 60% stocks / 40% bonds. After a rally, stocks are 70% of the portfolio. How much stock must be sold to restore the target?
e: Stocks now = 70% × $500,000 = $350,000. Target = 60% × $500,000 = $300,000. Sell $350,000 − $300,000 = $50,000 and buy bonds to restore 60/40.

q: How much is invested in emerging-market equity in this core-and-satellite portfolio?
e: Satellite = 20% × $1,200,000 = $240,000. Emerging-market equity = 30% × $240,000 = $72,000.
stem: $1,200,000 portfolio: 80% core (index funds), 20% satellite. Satellite split: 30% emerging-market equity, 25% REITs, 25% high-yield bonds, 20% commodities.

q: Which strategy best fits Lorraine's goals?
o: Contribute the shares to a diversified exchange fund
Gift the shares outright to her adult son
Sell the shares to the company's ESOP
Transfer the shares to a charitable remainder trust
e: A CRT creates a charitable income tax deduction that can offset compensation income, and because the trust is tax-exempt it can sell the shares without income tax, then diversify.
stem: Lorraine, 58, a public-company executive, holds most of her wealth in low-basis employer stock. She is charitably inclined, wants a current income tax deduction to offset her high compensation, and wants the stock sold and diversified without the sale itself being taxed.

q: A global pandemic triggers a sharp market selloff. How does the textbook classify this source of risk?
o: Exogenous
Endogenous
Unsystematic
Incremental
e: Exogenous risks are non-financial catastrophes from outside the financial system (terror attacks, earthquakes, tsunamis, pandemics) that slow commerce and create fear.

q: Which client event most clearly calls for redesigning the investment policy statement?
o: Receiving a 4% raise at her annual performance review
Unexpectedly inheriting a business worth triple her portfolio
A sudden 6% one-week drop in the S&P 500 Index
Her bond fund trailing its benchmark slightly this quarter
e: A sudden large inheritance is discontinuous change: a radical break in the client's economic life that requires reassessing IPS assumptions and strategies. Noise is ignored; incremental change is watched.

q: During a sharp bear market, Corinne, 44, with a long time horizon and a 75/25 stock/bond IPS, demands to sell her stocks. Which advisor response best fits the textbook?
o: Move her to cash now and re-enter once volatility subsides
Shift the portfolio to all Treasuries until the economy recovers
Listen, reassure, revisit the IPS, and keep the allocation
Switch to tactical allocation so she can time the rebound
e: When a client insists on raising cash, the best course is usually no action: keep a long-term view and the existing allocation. Markets have a long-term positive bias, and the IPS should transcend current conditions.

q: Before any crisis, which step best prepares a client to absorb a sudden job loss without disrupting the long-term portfolio?
o: Count on federal stimulus programs being offered again
Hold a large single-stock position as a flexible reserve
Plan to borrow on margin against the stock portfolio
Keep liquid reserves such as a money market account
e: Regular access to liquid investments, such as a money market account, lets clients meet short-term setbacks without selling long-term holdings at depressed prices.

q: After vivid news coverage of a market crash, a client becomes convinced another one is imminent. Which heuristic is most likely at work?
o: Availability
Anchoring and adjustment
Familiarity
Overconfidence
e: The availability heuristic leads investors to overweight vivid or recent events, such as fearing a crash after dramatic coverage. Recognizing it helps the advisor keep the client on plan.

stem:
Calloway case. Graham (53) and Nadia (50) are drafting an IPS. Two items on their list:

  • Keep a cash reserve equal to six months of living expenses.
  • Have Leah’s first-year college money available when she starts college in three years.
q: In which section of the Calloways' investment policy statement (IPS) should these two needs be recorded?
o: Return requirement
Liquidity
Laws and regulations
Permitted and excluded investments
e: Liquidity constraints record money the clients must be able to reach: an emergency reserve and any known outlay within roughly the next three to five years, such as tuition. Many advisors keep money needed inside five years out of the stock market. The return requirement states the target return; laws and regulations mainly concern plans like ERISA trusts; permitted/excluded investments lists the clients’ preferences.

stem: Calloway case. Net worth about $2.05 million; combined salaries $350,000; adequate life and disability coverage; about 12 years to retirement. In a past bear market Graham sold most of his stock funds near the low, and he says a 15% portfolio drop would cost him sleep. The planner calculates that their retirement goal needs a 6.5% annual return.
q: Which statement best describes the Calloways' risk tolerance for the IPS?
o: Low ability and low willingness; the IPS should target capital preservation and leave the 6.5% goal as is
High ability and high willingness; their net worth lets the IPS set above-average volatility
Low ability but high willingness; the planner should rely on the questionnaire score alone
High ability but low willingness; the IPS should record both and reconcile the risk level with the 6.5% requirement
e: Ability depends on resources and circumstances (wealth, income, insurance, horizon), and the Calloways’ is high. Willingness is emotional comfort with swings, and Graham’s history shows it is low. The IPS addresses both, and the risk objective must fit the return requirement: if 6.5% needs more risk than they will accept, they must accept more risk, lower the goal, or do some of each.

stem:
Calloway case. Living expenses run $13,500 per month, and the Calloways want a reserve equal to six months of living expenses. They have an annual cash-flow surplus of $47,600.

Liquid assetBalance
Checking account$18,000
Money market mutual fund$24,000
1-year bank CD$20,000

Other resources: taxable brokerage $542,060; 401(k)s $705,000; a home equity line of credit is available.
q: How large is the gap in the Calloways' emergency reserve, and what is the best way to close it?
o: $19,000; add it to a money market holding from the cash-flow surplus or taxable assets
$19,000; arrange a 401(k) loan that can be drawn if an emergency occurs
$81,000; open a home equity line of credit to serve as the whole reserve
$39,000; leave the CD out of the reserve and draw the gap from the 401(k)s
e: Target = 6 × $13,500 = $81,000. Liquid assets = $18,000 + $24,000 + $20,000 = $62,000. Gap = $81,000 − $62,000 = $19,000. The reserve belongs in highly liquid, marketable holdings such as a money market account so short-term setbacks never force a sale of long-term assets or new borrowing. Their $47,600 surplus can fill the gap within the year.

stem: Calloway case. Nadia plans to hold the new reserve money in the Pinecrest Money Market Fund, a money market mutual fund at their brokerage. She says it is “just as safe as a bank money market account because both are FDIC insured.”
q: Which response by the planner is most accurate?
o: She is right; both accounts carry FDIC coverage up to $250,000 per ownership category
She is right only if the fund holds Treasury bills, which makes the fund itself FDIC insured
The mutual fund is not federally insured; a bank money market deposit account is insured up to $250,000 per ownership category
Neither account is insured, but only the bank account permits check-writing
e: Money market mutual funds are offered by open-end investment companies and are not federally insured, although they hold high-quality short-term paper and are very liquid. A money market deposit account (MMDA) is a bank obligation insured up to $250,000 per ownership category (2026 edition figure). Either can hold an emergency fund; the client simply needs to know the difference.

stem: Calloway case. When their $20,000 CD matures, Nadia wants to roll it into 13-week Treasury bills yielding 4.0%. The Calloways are in the 32% federal bracket and a 5% state bracket. Inflation is expected to run 3.0%.
q: What is the Calloways' after-tax, inflation-adjusted return on the T-bills?
o: −0.27%
−0.47%
e: T-bill interest is federally taxed but state-exempt, so use 32% only (2026 edition figure). After-tax = 4.0% × (1 − 0.32) = 2.72%. Real = [(1.0272 ÷ 1.03) − 1] × 100 = −0.27%. The roll-over keeps reserve money safe but loses purchasing power: fine for an emergency fund, a poor home for long-term money.

stem: Calloway case. Six months after the IPS is signed, stocks fall 25% in two months. Graham, 53, wants to move his entire 401(k) ($410,000) into the stable value fund “until things calm down.” The six-month reserve is fully funded, both spouses still have their jobs, and retirement is about 12 years away.
q: What is the planner's best course of action with Graham?
o: Keep a long-term perspective and hold the IPS allocation, reminding Graham why it was chosen
Move the 401(k) to stable value now and re-enter after the market regains half its loss
Shift half the 401(k) to stable value as a compromise to ease Graham’s anxiety
Rewrite the IPS around capital preservation because a 25% decline changes their goals
e: With jobs, reserves and a 12-year horizon intact, the decline is market turmoil, not a change in the clients’ own situation. When a client presses to move to cash, the best course is usually no action: keep the allocation and the long view. Markets carry a long-term positive bias that rewards patient, diversified investors; abandoning the plan tends to leave clients on the sidelines early in a recovery.

stem:
Calloway case. Over the next year the planner notes these events:

  • I. Graham receives a 4% raise.
  • II. The S&P 500 drops 2% in one week, then recovers.
  • III. Kestrel eliminates Nadia’s division; she is laid off with six months of severance.
q: Which event(s) should prompt the planner to reassess the assumptions in the Calloways' IPS?
o: I and III
II and III
III only
I, II, and III
e: Change comes in three kinds. Noise (II) carries no meaning and is ignored. Incremental change (I) is a small extension of an existing pattern and bears watching. Discontinuous change (III), such as losing a job, is a radical break that calls for revisiting the IPS assumptions: income, liquidity, risk capacity and the Kestrel holding.

stem: Calloway case. Graham wants low-cost index funds that track broad markets, with little trading. Nadia wants part of the money in actively chosen, higher-risk areas (emerging markets and REITs) that might beat the market. Both want diversification and attention to taxes.
q: Which approach best reconciles the spouses' preferences for their retirement assets?
o: Tactical asset allocation applied to the entire portfolio
A single moderate model portfolio from a fund sponsor’s questionnaire
A strategic allocation held entirely in index funds with no active component
A core-and-satellite strategy: a passive index core plus a smaller active satellite sleeve
e: Core and satellite puts most assets in passive broad-market index funds (the core, run strategically) and a smaller share in higher-risk opportunities such as emerging markets, REITs or high-yield bonds (the satellite, run tactically). Its aims (diversification, returns in line with the required return, low transaction costs, tax management) fit both spouses.

stem: Calloway case. Nadia holds 4,000 shares of her employer, Kestrel Diagnostics (KDX), worth $90 per share ($360,000), with a basis of $40 per share. KDX is about 25% of the couple’s investment assets. She wants to diversify without an immediate capital gains tax, and she wants the value to stay with the family rather than go to charity.
q: Which strategy best meets Nadia's goals for her Kestrel shares?
o: Contribute the shares to an exchange fund
Transfer the shares to a charitable remainder trust
Give the shares to Leah and Sam
Sell the shares and buy a diversified index fund
e: An exchange fund takes concentrated public stock in return for a proportional interest in a diversified pool, spreading the company-specific (unsystematic) risk without an immediate capital gains tax, and Nadia keeps the value. A CRT avoids tax on the sale but leaves the remainder to charity; gifting gives up ownership; an outright sale taxes the $200,000 gain (4,000 × $50).

stem: Calloway case. Nadia owns 4,000 KDX shares at $90. Worried about a drop before Kestrel’s next product decision, she buys 40 six-month KDX put contracts with an $80 strike at a premium of $2.50 per share. She is not a corporate insider and has no trading restrictions.
q: Ignoring commissions, what is the minimum net value of Nadia's hedged KDX position at expiration (the value the puts lock in, less the premium paid)?
e: Premium = 40 contracts × 100 × $2.50 = $10,000. However far KDX falls, she can sell at $80: 4,000 × $80 = $320,000. Net floor = $320,000 − $10,000 = $310,000, versus $360,000 today. A protective put works like insurance: she keeps the upside, but the cost recurs and coverage ends at expiration.

stem: Calloway case. Nadia finds the puts too costly to renew every six months. She wants to protect KDX (now $90) against a fall below $80 with no net premium outlay, and she is willing to give up gains above $105.
q: Which option position should Nadia add to her 4,000 KDX shares?
o: Buy 40 $80 puts and write 40 $105 calls with offsetting premiums
Write 40 $105 covered calls and nothing else
Write 40 $80 puts and buy 40 $105 calls
Buy 40 $90 calls and 40 $90 puts (a long straddle)
e: A zero-cost collar = long stock + long put + short call. The $80 put sets a floor; the premium received for the $105 call pays for the put, so the net cost is about zero. The trade-off: shares may be called away above $105. Covered calls alone cap the upside but give only premium-sized protection in a sharp drop.

stem: Calloway case. Planning assumptions: 13-week T-bill (risk-free) rate 4.0%; expected market return 10.0%. KDX has a beta of 1.40. Analysts’ consensus expected return for KDX is 11.0%.
q: Using the CAPM, what is the required return on KDX, and what does it imply about adding to the position?
o: 18.0%; KDX is undervalued, so buy more
12.4%; the expected return falls short, so do not add to KDX
8.4%; the expected return exceeds it, so add to KDX
14.0%; KDX plots on the security market line, so hold it unchanged
e: CAPM: r = r<sub>f</sub> + (r<sub>m</sub> − r<sub>f</sub>)β = 4.0% + (10.0% − 4.0%)(1.40) = 4.0% + 8.4% = 12.4%. Its high turnover can produce capital gains distributions taxable to the Calloways. III. The expense ratio already includes the fund's brokerage commissions. IV. The manager's departure is a reason to monitor the fund more closely.
o: I and III
II and IV
I, II, and IV

e: Turnover generates commissions, bid-ask spreads and market-impact costs, none of which appear in the expense ratio (I true; III false, since the ratio covers operating expenses, management fees and 12b-1 fees). stem: Calloway case. On December 12 the Calloways sell their entire Harborline position for $85,000 (basis $100,000). On January 2, 21 days later, Graham buys Harborline again in the same account for $82,000.
q: What loss can the Calloways recognize on the December sale, and what is their basis in the repurchased shares?
o: $0 loss; basis $97,000
$0 loss; basis $82,000
e: Buying the same security within 30 days before or after selling it at a loss (2026 edition figure) is a wash sale. The $15,000 loss ($85,000 − $100,000) is postponed, not lost: it is added to the new shares’ basis, $82,000 + $15,000 = $97,000. Waiting more than 30 days to buy Harborline back would have kept the loss deductible.

q: Which change makes the Calloways' asset placement most tax-efficient while keeping their overall stock/bond mix?
o: Hold the taxable bond exposure in the 401(k) and keep tax-efficient index funds or municipals in the joint account
Buy municipal bonds inside Nadia’s Roth IRA so the bond income is doubly tax-free
Keep the bond fund in the joint account, since its interest is taxed the same in any account

e: Tax-inefficient holdings (taxable interest, nonqualified dividends, high turnover) are best kept in tax-deferred accounts; tax-efficient ones (broad index funds, qualified dividends, municipals) can sit in taxable accounts. q: Using the duration formula, approximately what will the Calloways' Ridgeway position be worth after the rate increase?
e: ΔP ÷ P = −D × [Δy ÷ (1 + y)] = −6.2 × (0.01 ÷ 1.052) = −5.89%. Change = −0.0589 × $60,000 ≈ −$3,536, so the value is about $56,464. The rule of thumb (6.2 × 1%) gives $56,280. A bond fund never matures, so this price risk cannot be removed by holding on.

stem: Calloway case. Leah, 15, starts college in three years. Her education account ($96,000, a taxable account in her parents’ names) is 100% in a stock index fund. The Calloways want to be confident the money will be there when the first bill arrives.
q: Which fixed-income approach best protects the money for Leah's first tuition bill?
o: A long-term bond fund with a duration of 14, for its higher yield
Three-year Treasury zero-coupon bonds, whose duration equals the three-year horizon
A barbell of 1-year and 20-year bonds
Keep the stock index fund, since stocks beat bonds over long periods
e: Matching a portfolio’s duration to the time until the money is needed immunizes it: higher rates lower prices but raise reinvestment income, and vice versa. A zero-coupon bond’s duration equals its maturity, so a 3-year Treasury zero delivers a known sum on schedule with no default or reinvestment risk. In a taxable account the accrued interest is taxed yearly (phantom income).

stem: Calloway case. One year ago the Calloways invested $36,000 in the unhedged Summit European Equity Fund when €1 = $1.08. Over the year the fund’s value in euros rose 9%, and the exchange rate is now €1 = $1.02. Ignore distributions.
q: What was the Calloways' holding period return on the Summit fund in U.S. dollars?
e: Convert at both ends: $36,000 ÷ 1.08 = €33,333; × 1.09 = €36,333; × $1.02 = $37,060. HPR = ($37,060 − $36,000) ÷ $36,000 = 2.94%, or 1.09 × (1.02 ÷ 1.08) − 1. The euro fell against the dollar, shrinking a 9% local gain to about 3%. A U.S. investor abroad wants the dollar to fall during the holding period.
